title: Programming from Zero

mentor.name: NULL-0
mentor.character: Never assumes you know anything, never talks down to you.

summary: Write, read and fix a real Python program. Start at the first line of code and finish building a tool you actually use.

lessons.title: The first line that runs
lessons.goal: You can write a line of Python that puts text on the console.
lessons.theory:
A Python program is a list of instructions. The machine reads them and does them. Nothing more mystical than that.

The instruction that makes a program say something is `print`. You write the word, then parentheses, and inside the parentheses you put what you want sent out:

```python
print("boot")
```

The quotes matter. Anything between quotes is **text**, and Python sends it out exactly as written. Without quotes Python would think you were naming something it should already know, and it would stop. Single or double quotes both work, as long as the one you open is the one you close.

What comes out lands in the **console**: the text panel next to your code. That panel is not decoration. For the rest of this track it is the only way you find out what your program actually did, as opposed to what you believed it would do.
lessons.task: The program already prints `boot`. Add a second line below it that prints the text `SYSTEM online`.
lessons.starter: print("boot")
lessons.solution:
print("boot")
print("SYSTEM online")
lessons.hint: Copy the shape of the line that is already there and change what sits between the quotes.

lessons.title: The console reads top to bottom
lessons.goal: You can predict the order in which a program prints, and use that order to see how far it got.
lessons.theory:
Instructions run in the order you wrote them: first line, then the next, then the next. There is no cleverness hiding in there. Each `print` ends its own line, so three prints give you three lines in the console, in the same order as the code.

That makes the console a **transcript**, not a screen. It is a record of what happened, in sequence, and it stays there after the program ends.

This is the whole basis of debugging, and you already have it. When a program misbehaves, the last line printed tells you the furthest point it reached. Everything above that line ran. Whatever comes after it did not. A log that jumps straight from `render: start` to `render: done` cannot tell you which step in the middle was slow or wrong, because nobody wrote a line for the middle.
lessons.task: The log jumps from the start of the render to the end. Insert one line between the two existing ones that prints `render: encoding`, so the transcript shows the middle step.
lessons.starter:
print("render: start")
print("render: done")
lessons.solution:
print("render: start")
print("render: encoding")
print("render: done")
lessons.hint: Where you put the new line in the code is where its text will appear in the console.

check.expects:
render: start
render: encoding
render: done

lessons.title: Several values in one line
lessons.goal: You can print text and a number side by side without stitching them together by hand.
lessons.theory:
`print` accepts more than one value. Separate them with commas and they all go out on the same line:

```python
print("channel", "Cobly")
```

Python puts **one space between each value** and one line break at the end. You do not add those yourself, and if you do you get two spaces.

Numbers are written without quotes: `12` is a number, `"12"` is text that happens to look like a number. In this mission the difference does not show up in the console, since both come out as the same characters. It will matter the moment you try to add them together, and that is chapter one's problem.

The order of the values is the order they appear on the line. Left to right, no surprises.
lessons.task: Add a second line that prints, in one single `print`, the word `pending`, then the number 12, then the word `jobs`, separated by commas.
lessons.starter: print("queue check")
lessons.solution:
print("queue check")
print("pending", 12, "jobs")
lessons.hint: One print, three values, two commas. The number is the only one without quotes.

lessons.title: A line Python ignores
lessons.goal: You can leave a note in the code and switch a line off without deleting it.
lessons.theory:
A `#` tells Python to ignore the rest of that line. The line still sits in the file, it just never runs. That is a **comment**.

It has two uses, and they are different jobs. The first is a note for whoever reads the code next, which is usually you in three months. The second is switching a line off, called **commenting out**: you put a `#` in front of a working line so it stops running, and you can bring it back later by removing the `#`. Deleting the line would work too, and then it would be gone.

One rule about the notes, because bad comments are worse than none. A comment that restates the line under it is noise:

```python
# print the queue
print("queue: 3 jobs")
```

That teaches the reader nothing they could not get from the code itself. A comment earns its place when it says something the code cannot: why the line is there, why it is switched off, what would break if someone removed it.
lessons.task: The debug line does not belong in the log any more, but you may want it back. Comment it out instead of deleting it, and put the note `# kept for the next payload bug` on the line above it.
lessons.starter:
print("upload: start")
print("debug: payload 8f2a")
print("upload: done")
lessons.solution:
print("upload: start")
# kept for the next payload bug
# print("debug: payload 8f2a")
print("upload: done")
lessons.hint: You add two characters in total: one `#` in front of the debug line, and one whole new line that starts with `#`.

value: # kept for the next payload bug

lessons.title: An error is a message
lessons.goal: You can read a Python error, find the line it points at, and fix it.
lessons.theory:
When Python cannot do what a line says, it stops and prints a **traceback**. It looks alarming and it is not. It is the machine telling you where it got stuck and why:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 2, in <module>
    print(ready)
NameError: name 'ready' is not defined
```

Read it from the **bottom up**. The last line is the one that matters: an error type, then a detail. `NameError` means Python found a bare word and expected it to be the name of something it already knows. It does not know `ready`, because nothing ever gave that word a meaning. The word was meant as text, and text goes in quotes. Above that, `line 2` is where to look.

The program stops at the failing line, and everything printed before it still happened. That is why the console is evidence: the lines that made it out mark how far you got, and the traceback marks the step that stopped you.

An error is the most useful output a program can give you. It names the file, the line and the problem. Compare that to a program that runs fine and quietly writes the wrong number to a report.
lessons.task: The last line of the log is commented out because it crashes with `NameError: name 'ready' is not defined`. Rewrite it as a working line that prints the text `ready`.
lessons.starter:
print("checks: 3 passed")
# print(ready)
lessons.solution:
print("checks: 3 passed")
print("ready")
lessons.hint: Python read `ready` as a name. Make it text instead.

lessons.title: A name for a value
lessons.goal: Store a value under a name and read it back later.
lessons.theory:
A **variable** is a name attached to a value. You write the name, then `=`, then the value: `channel = "Cobly"`. From that line on, wherever you write `channel`, Python hands you the value back.

The `=` is not the equals of mathematics. It does not claim that two things are the same. It is an order with a direction: evaluate the thing on the right, then make the name on the left point at it.

A name must start with a letter or an underscore and cannot contain spaces. `channel_name` is a valid name, `channel name` is two names and an error. Python is case sensitive, so `Channel` and `channel` are different names.

Printing a variable prints the value it holds, not the name. `print(channel)` prints Cobly. `print("channel")` prints the word channel, because the quotes turn it into text.
lessons.task: Keep the line that is already there. Below it, create a variable called `channel` holding the text Altos del Bosque Nocturno, and print that variable.
lessons.starter: print("Channel report")
lessons.solution:
print("Channel report")
channel = "Altos del Bosque Nocturno"
print(channel)
lessons.hint: Two more lines: one that puts the text into `channel`, one that passes `channel` to `print` with no quotes around it.

check.expects:
Channel report
Altos del Bosque Nocturno

lessons.title: Text between quotes
lessons.goal: Build one piece of text out of several.
lessons.theory:
A **string** is text. You mark it with quotes, single or double, and you close it with the same one you opened: `"Pluma"` and `'Pluma'` are the same value.

The quotes are not part of the value. They are how you tell Python where the text starts and ends. Without them Python reads `Pluma` as a variable name and stops, because no such name exists.

`+` between two strings joins them into a new string. It joins exactly what you give it and adds nothing of its own: `"Pluma" + "Waves"` is `PlumaWaves`. If you want a space between them, you pass one, as a string of its own: `"Pluma" + " " + "Waves"`.

Joining changes nothing. `first + second` builds a third string and leaves `first` and `second` exactly as they were. If you want to keep the result, give it a name.
lessons.task: Join `first`, a space, and `second` into a new variable called `full`, and print `full` instead of `first`.
lessons.starter:
first = "Pluma"
second = "Waves"
print(first)
lessons.solution:
first = "Pluma"
second = "Waves"
full = first + " " + second
print(full)
lessons.hint: The space is a string too, so it needs its own quotes.

lessons.title: Whole numbers and decimals
lessons.goal: Do arithmetic with variables and know which type comes out.
lessons.theory:
Numbers are written without quotes. `12` is an **int**, a whole number. `7.5` is a **float**, a number with a decimal point. `"12"` is neither, it is a string that happens to look like a number.

The usual operators work between numbers: `+`, `-`, `*` for multiplication and `/` for division. You can use them on variables exactly as on literal numbers, because Python reads the value out of the name first.

`/` always produces a float, even when the division comes out even: `10 / 5` is `5.0`, not `5`. That trailing `.0` is not a mistake, it is Python telling you the type of the result.

The result of an expression disappears unless you keep it. `minutes / videos` on its own line computes a number and throws it away. Assign it to a name to use it later.
lessons.task: Divide `minutes` by `videos`, store the result in a variable called `average`, and print `average` instead of `videos`.
lessons.starter:
videos = 12
minutes = 90
print(videos)
lessons.solution:
videos = 12
minutes = 90
average = minutes / videos
print(average)
lessons.hint: Minutes divided by videos, in that order, with the whole expression on the right of the `=`.

lessons.title: Values inside text
lessons.goal: Write one sentence that carries the contents of several variables.
lessons.theory:
An **f-string** is a string with an `f` in front of the opening quote. Inside it, anything you put between `{` and `}` is not text: Python evaluates it and drops the result in.

```
channel = "Cobly"
print(f"scanning {channel}")
```

That prints `scanning Cobly`. Without the `f`, the braces stay as braces and you get `scanning {channel}` printed literally.

This is why f-strings replace joining with `+` for anything real. `+` demands strings on both sides and refuses to join a string to a number. An f-string converts whatever is in the braces to text for you, so numbers, strings and both together work with no ceremony.

You can put as many pairs of braces as you want in one f-string, and normal text between them.
lessons.task: Replace the last line with a single f-string that prints `Cobly has 188000 subscribers`, taking both values out of the variables rather than typing them again.
lessons.starter:
channel = "Cobly"
subscribers = 188000
print(channel)
lessons.solution:
channel = "Cobly"
subscribers = 188000
print(f"{channel} has {subscribers} subscribers")
lessons.hint: One `f` before the opening quote, and each variable name wrapped in braces where its value belongs.

lessons.title: One name, a new value
lessons.goal: Change what a name points at, and know what happened to the old value.
lessons.theory:
A name holds one value at a time. Assigning to a name that already exists does not create a second one, it repoints the same name and the previous value is gone.

```
pending = 4
pending = 3
```

After those two lines there is one name and one value. Nothing remembers the `4`.

The line `pending = pending - 1` looks circular and is not, because the two sides run at different moments. The right side is evaluated **first**, using the value the name has right now, which gives `3`. Only then does the name get repointed at that result. Read every assignment that way: right side first, name second.

This is the whole mechanism behind counters, totals and anything that accumulates. There is no magic in it, only a name being repointed one line at a time.
lessons.task: After the line that is already there, subtract 1 from `pending` and store it back in `pending`, then print the same f-string again so the second value shows.
lessons.starter:
pending = 4
print(f"pending: {pending}")
lessons.solution:
pending = 4
print(f"pending: {pending}")
pending = pending - 1
print(f"pending: {pending}")
lessons.hint: `pending` appears on both sides of the `=`, and the print line below is a copy of the one above.

lessons.title: Asking Python what a value is
lessons.goal: Find out the type of any value instead of guessing it.
lessons.theory:
Every value has a type, and the type decides what the value can do. `+` between two ints adds them. `+` between two strings glues them. Same operator, different behaviour, chosen entirely by the types involved.

`type(x)` answers the question. You pass it a value or a variable and it hands back the type:

```
print(type(90))
```

That prints `<class 'int'>`. A string gives `<class 'str'>` and a decimal gives `<class 'float'>`. The `class` wording is Python vocabulary you will meet properly much later, for now read it as "this is an int".

Use it when a program misbehaves on data that looks correct. A number read from a file, a form or a command line is very often a string wearing a number's clothes, and `type()` is how you catch it in one line instead of guessing for twenty minutes.
lessons.task: Replace the last line with two lines: one that prints the type of `views`, and one that prints the type of `label`.
lessons.starter:
views = 3800000
label = "Cobly"
print(views)
lessons.solution:
views = 3800000
label = "Cobly"
print(type(views))
print(type(label))
lessons.hint: `type(...)` goes inside `print(...)`, so there are two sets of brackets on each line.

lessons.title: Turning one type into another
lessons.goal: Convert a string into a number so you can do arithmetic with it.
lessons.theory:
`int("142")` gives the number `142`. `str(142)` gives the text `"142"`. `float("7.5")` gives the decimal `7.5`. Each one **returns a new value** and leaves the original untouched, so the result is worth nothing unless you assign it to a name or use it immediately.

You need this because Python refuses to mix types silently. `"142" + 8` does not give `150` and does not give `"1428"`, it raises a `TypeError`, because Python will not guess which of the two you meant.

Conversion can fail, and when it does it fails loudly. `int("abc")` raises a `ValueError`, and so does `int("7.5")`, because that text is not a whole number. `float("7.5")` is the one that works there.

The habit worth building: convert once, at the edge where the text arrives, and keep numbers as numbers everywhere after that.
lessons.task: Convert `count_text` into a whole number, store it in a variable called `count`, and print `count + 8`.
lessons.starter:
count_text = "142"
print(count_text)
lessons.solution:
count_text = "142"
count = int(count_text)
print(count + 8)
lessons.hint: Convert on its own line first, then do the arithmetic inside `print`.

lessons.title: Reading what you type
lessons.goal: Take a value from outside the program while it is running.
lessons.theory:
`input()` stops the program, waits until a line is typed and Enter is pressed, and returns that line. It is the first thing you have written whose result is not decided by your own code.

What comes back is **always a string**. If the person types `8`, you get `"8"`, not `8`. Nothing about the appearance of the text changes that, which is why the previous mission exists: text that arrives from outside gets converted the moment it arrives.

The returned line does not include the Enter, and it disappears unless you keep it, exactly like any other expression. `input()` alone on a line reads a value and throws it away.

You can pass a prompt inside the brackets, `input("Channel name: ")`, or print the prompt on its own line first. Both are fine, the second keeps the two jobs visibly separate.
lessons.task: Read a line with `input()` into a variable called `name`, and change the last line into an f-string that prints `scanning` followed by that name.
lessons.starter:
print("Channel name:")
print("scanning")
lessons.solution:
print("Channel name:")
name = input()
print(f"scanning {name}")
lessons.hint: `input()` takes no arguments here, and its result goes on the right of an `=`.

check.expects:
Channel name:
scanning Pluma Waves Soundscapes

lessons.title: Names that explain themselves
lessons.goal: Choose names that make the next reader understand the code without running it.
lessons.theory:
`x = 8` is legal and tells you nothing. Six weeks later you will not know whether 8 is videos, minutes, retries or a day of the month, and you will have to reconstruct it from the lines around it.

A good name says what the value **is**, and its unit when it has one. `videos_per_day` beats `videos` beats `v`. `total_minutes` beats `total`. Python convention is lowercase words joined by underscores, which reads well and takes no thought.

Two rules that catch most bad names. Do not abbreviate anything the reader would have to decode: `vpd` saves nine characters and costs a lookup every single time. Do not name a thing after its type: `number_variable` says what Python already knows and hides what you actually meant.

Renaming is nearly free now and expensive later, when the same bad name has spread into thirty lines. Fix it the moment it bothers you.
lessons.task: Rewrite the program with real names: read the count with `int(input())` into `videos_per_day`, keep 45 in `minutes_each`, multiply them into `total_minutes`, and print `8 videos, 360 minutes` with one f-string.
lessons.starter:
x = 8
y = 45
print(x * y)
lessons.solution:
videos_per_day = int(input())
minutes_each = 45
total_minutes = videos_per_day * minutes_each
print(f"{videos_per_day} videos, {total_minutes} minutes")
lessons.hint: Four lines, one per job: read, store, multiply, print. The two numbers in the sentence both come out of variables.

lessons.title: True and False are values
lessons.goal: You can store a yes/no fact in a variable and check that its type is bool.
lessons.theory:
`True` and `False` are values, exactly like `7` or `"draft"`. You can put them in a variable, print them and pass them around. The capital letter is not optional: `true` is not a Python value, and writing it gets you `NameError: name 'true' is not defined`.

They have a type of their own. `type(True)` reports `<class 'bool'>`, short for **boolean**. A bool has exactly two values and nothing else. That is the whole point: it answers one question with no room for a maybe.

Everything in this chapter runs on bools. A program decides by asking a question that can only come back `True` or `False`, and then doing one thing or the other. Before you can decide anything, you need to be comfortable holding the answer in a variable.
lessons.task: Add a variable `upload_finished` set to `False`. Print `channel_is_live`, then print `upload_finished`, then print the type of `upload_finished`.
lessons.starter:
channel_is_live = True
print(channel_is_live)
lessons.solution:
channel_is_live = True
upload_finished = False
print(channel_is_live)
print(upload_finished)
print(type(upload_finished))
lessons.hint: `type(x)` was in the last chapter, and it works on a bool the same way it works on a number.

lessons.title: Comparing two values
lessons.goal: You can turn two numbers into a True or False answer with a comparison operator.
lessons.theory:
You rarely type `True` by hand. You produce it by comparing two things. Python has six comparison operators and every one of them hands back a bool:

- `==` equal to
- `!=` not equal to
- `<` less than
- `>` greater than
- `<=` less than or equal
- `>=` greater than or equal

The one that bites everybody is `==`. A single `=` **assigns**: `views = 4200` puts a number into a name. A double `==` **asks**: `views == 4200` returns `True` or `False` and changes nothing. They look alike and do opposite jobs.

A comparison is an expression, like `2 + 2`. It has a value, so you can print it, store it in a variable, or hand it to the `if` you will meet in the next mission.
lessons.task: Keep the line that prints `views`. Then print the result of comparing `views < target`, and on the next line the result of `views == target`.
lessons.starter:
views = 4200
target = 10000
print(views)
lessons.solution:
views = 4200
target = 10000
print(views)
print(views < target)
print(views == target)
lessons.hint: Put the whole comparison inside `print(...)`, the same way you would print `2 + 2`.

lessons.title: Running code only when it matters
lessons.goal: You can make a block of code run only when a condition is True.
lessons.theory:
`if` takes a condition and a block. If the condition is `True`, the block runs. If it is `False`, the block is skipped entirely, and the program carries on with the next line at the outer level.

The shape is fixed:

```
if free_slots == 0:
    print("queue is full")
```

Two details are not decoration. The **colon** ends the condition line. The **indentation**, four spaces, is what marks the block as belonging to the `if`. Python has no braces; the whitespace is the syntax. Forget the colon and you get `SyntaxError: expected ':'`. Indent by accident and you get `IndentationError: unexpected indent`.

Everything at the same indent level belongs to the same block. Two indented lines under one `if` both run or both are skipped, together.
lessons.task: Under the existing print, add an `if` that checks whether `free_slots` equals 0 and, when it does, prints `queue is full`.
lessons.starter:
free_slots = 0
print(f"free slots: {free_slots}")
lessons.solution:
free_slots = 0
print(f"free slots: {free_slots}")
if free_slots == 0:
    print("queue is full")
lessons.hint: Condition line ends in a colon, and the print below it is indented four spaces.

lessons.title: The other branch
lessons.goal: You can give an if a second block that runs when the condition is False.
lessons.theory:
`else` attaches to an `if` and holds the code for the other case. Exactly one of the two blocks runs, never both, never neither. There is no condition after `else`, only a colon, because its condition is already decided: whatever the `if` was not.

```
if minutes_watched >= 4000:
    print("threshold reached")
else:
    print("still short")
```

`else` must sit at the same indent level as its `if`, with nothing between them but the `if` block. Line them up in the same column and read them as one unit: one question, two answers.

An `if` with no `else` is fine when the other case needs nothing done. Write `else` when the other case needs something done, not out of symmetry.
lessons.task: Add an `else` to the existing `if` so that when the threshold is not reached the program prints `still short`.
lessons.hint: `else:` goes in the same column as `if`, and its print is indented four spaces under it.

lessons.title: More than two answers
lessons.goal: You can chain several conditions so the first true one wins.
lessons.theory:
`elif` is short for *else if*. It goes between the `if` and the `else`, and you can have as many as you need. Python checks the conditions from top to bottom, runs the block of the **first** one that is `True`, and then jumps past the whole chain without looking at the rest.

```
if temperature >= 100:
    print("critical")
elif temperature >= 90:
    print("hot, pausing")
else:
    print("normal")
```

Because the first match wins, **order is the logic**. Put `>= 90` above `>= 100` and a temperature of 105 reports as merely hot: it matched the loose test first and the strict one never ran. When your conditions overlap, the strictest goes on top.

The `else` at the bottom is optional, but a chain without one silently does nothing when no condition matches. Ask yourself whether that silence is what you want.
lessons.task: Insert an `elif` between the `if` and the `else` that catches a `temperature` of 90 or more and prints `hot, pausing`.
lessons.hint: The new branch sits in the same column as `if` and `else`, and 96 must match it before the `else` is ever reached.

lessons.title: Combining conditions
lessons.goal: You can join two conditions with and or or, and flip one with not.
lessons.theory:
Three words build every compound condition you will ever write.

- `a and b` is `True` only when **both** are true.
- `a or b` is `True` when **at least one** is true. It is not the exclusive or of everyday speech: if both are true, the answer is still `True`.
- `not a` flips the value. `not True` is `False`.

They work on the bools you already have and on comparisons: `views > 1000 and duration >= 60` is one condition made of two.

Read `and` as a chain that a single `False` breaks, and `or` as a chain that a single `True` saves. When a compound condition gets long enough that you have to read it twice, store the halves in named variables first and combine the names. `script_ready and voice_ready` explains itself; four comparisons glued together do not.
lessons.task: Keep the first print. Then print whether all three pieces are ready using `and`, then whether the script or the images are ready using `or`, then whether the images are still missing using `not`.
lessons.starter:
has_script = True
has_voice = True
has_images = False
print(has_script and has_voice)
lessons.solution:
has_script = True
has_voice = True
has_images = False
print(has_script and has_voice)
print(has_script and has_voice and has_images)
print(has_script or has_images)
print(not has_images)
lessons.hint: You can chain more than two: `a and b and c` is a single condition.

lessons.title: A decision inside a decision
lessons.goal: You can put an if inside another if, and you know why you should not go deep.
lessons.theory:
A block can contain anything, including another `if`. Each level indents four more spaces, and the inner condition is only ever asked when the outer one was true.

```
if api_key == "set":
    print("key found")
    if quota_left == 0:
        print("no quota, skipping")
```

That is legal and sometimes right. What is not right is a pyramid. At three or four levels, the line you are reading no longer tells you what has to be true for it to run: you have to climb back up through every condition above it and hold them all in your head at once. Bugs live in the branch nobody scrolled to.

There is also a cheap rewrite hiding in most nests. `if a: if b:` with nothing else in the outer block is the same thing as `if a and b:`, one level flatter. Two missions from now you will see the general version of that move.
lessons.task: Inside the existing `if`, under the print, add a nested `if` that prints `no quota, skipping` when `quota_left` equals 0.
lessons.starter:
api_key = "set"
quota_left = 0
if api_key == "set":
    print("key found")
lessons.hint: The inner `if` is indented four spaces, and its own print is indented eight.

lessons.title: Empty counts as false
lessons.goal: You can test a value directly, knowing which values Python already treats as false.
lessons.theory:
`if` does not require a bool. It accepts any value and decides whether that value is **truthy** or **falsy**. The falsy ones are few and worth memorising: `False`, `0`, `0.0`, the empty string `""`, and `None`. Everything else is truthy, including the string `"0"`, which is one character long and therefore not empty.

`bool(value)` shows you the verdict without an `if`. `bool("")` is `False`, `bool("draft")` is `True`, `bool(0)` is `False`, `bool(-1)` is `True`. Negative is not empty.

This is why `if not title:` is the normal way to say *the title is missing*. It is shorter than `if title == "":` and it also catches `None`. Use it when you mean **empty or absent**. When you mean **zero specifically**, write `== 0`, because a real 0 and a missing value are different problems and truthiness cannot tell them apart.
lessons.task: After the existing print, print `bool(title)`, then add an `if not title:` that prints `title is missing`.
lessons.starter:
title = ""
description = "Sleep frequencies, 3 hours"
print(bool(description))
lessons.solution:
title = ""
description = "Sleep frequencies, 3 hours"
print(bool(description))
print(bool(title))
if not title:
    print("title is missing")
lessons.hint: An empty string is falsy, so `not title` is `True` here.

lessons.title: Guard clauses flatten the pyramid
lessons.goal: You can rewrite a nested pile of checks as a flat chain that rejects the bad cases first.
lessons.theory:
A **guard clause** is a check that handles the bad case immediately and gets it out of the way, so the code below it can assume that case is gone. Instead of wrapping the good path in condition after condition, you list the reasons to stop, one per branch, and leave the good path alone at the bottom.

The starting code is the pyramid: three levels of nesting, and `"uploading"` buried eight spaces deep. The flat version says the same thing:

```
if quota_left == 0:
    print("no quota")
elif not file_ready:
    print("no file")
else:
    print("uploading")
```

Every branch is at one indent level. Each one reads as a complete sentence with no context above it, adding a new reason to stop costs one line instead of one level, and the success case is the last thing you read instead of the most hidden. Later, inside a function, each guard ends in `return` and the chain does not even need `elif`. The shape you are learning now is the same one.
lessons.task: Replace the nested `if` blocks with a flat chain that checks, in order: `quota_left == 0` prints `no quota`, `not file_ready` prints `no file`, `duration < 60` prints `too short`, `not thumbnail_ready` prints `no thumbnail`, and the `else` prints `uploading`.
lessons.hint: One `if`, three `elif`, one `else`, all five words in the same column, and nothing indented more than four spaces.

lessons.title: The loop that runs while something is true
lessons.goal: Repeat a block of code as long as a condition holds, and move the value that ends it.
lessons.theory:
Everything you have written so far runs once, top to bottom. Real work is not like that: a render is checked again and again until it is done, an upload is retried until it goes through. That is a **loop**.

`while` is the plainest one. You write `while` followed by a condition and a colon, and indent the block under it. Python tests the condition, runs the block if it is `True`, then tests it again. When the condition turns `False`, the loop stops and the program continues with the first line that is not indented.

A `while` loop has three parts and all three must be there:

- a value that exists **before** the loop, here `attempt = 1`
- a condition that reads that value, here `attempt <= 3`
- a line **inside** the loop that moves the value, here `attempt = attempt + 1`

Forget the third one and the condition stays true forever. That is the accident you will meet again in the last mission of this chapter.
lessons.task: Wrap the print in a `while` loop so it runs for attempts 1, 2 and 3, add the line that moves `attempt` forward, and print `giving up` after the loop ends.
lessons.starter:
attempt = 1
print(f"attempt {attempt}")
lessons.solution:
attempt = 1
while attempt <= 3:
    print(f"attempt {attempt}")
    attempt = attempt + 1
print("giving up")
lessons.hint: The `giving up` line is not indented, so it is outside the loop and runs once.

lessons.title: Counting turns with for and range
lessons.goal: Repeat a block a known number of times and use the turn number inside it.
lessons.theory:
`while` is for when you do not know how many turns you need. When you do know, `for` says it in one line.

`range(4)` produces the numbers 0, 1, 2, 3. Four numbers, starting at zero, stopping **before** the number you gave it. `for i in range(4):` runs the indented block once per number, and each time the name `i` holds the current one. You do not create `i` and you do not move it, the `for` does both.

Starting at zero looks wrong until you work with data. Positions in Python are counted from zero, so a loop that counts from zero lines up with them. When you want to show a human 1, 2, 3 you print `i + 1`, but the loop itself keeps counting from zero.
lessons.task: Replace the single print with a `for` loop over `range(clips)` that prints `rendering clip` followed by the number of the turn, then print `done` after the loop.
lessons.starter:
clips = 4
print("rendering clip")
lessons.solution:
clips = 4
for i in range(clips):
    print(f"rendering clip {i}")
print("done")
lessons.hint: `range()` accepts a variable, not only a literal number.

check.expects:
rendering clip 0
rendering clip 1
rendering clip 2
rendering clip 3
done

lessons.title: A range that starts and steps where you want
lessons.goal: Control the first number, the last number and the size of the jump in a range.
lessons.theory:
`range` takes up to three numbers. `range(stop)` counts from 0. `range(start, stop)` counts from `start`. `range(start, stop, step)` counts from `start` in jumps of `step`.

In every one of those, `stop` is the number the range never reaches. `range(6, 19, 4)` gives 6, 10, 14, 18 and then stops, because the next jump would be 22 and 22 is past 19. This looks like an off-by-one trap and it is the opposite: it means `range(0, 4)` has exactly 4 numbers in it, which is the thing you actually need when you count.

A negative `step` counts backwards: `range(10, 0, -1)` gives 10 down to 1.
lessons.task: Change the range so the loop prints an upload window at 6, 10, 14 and 18, by giving `range` a start, a stop and a step.
lessons.starter:
for hour in range(6):
    print(f"upload window at {hour}:00")
lessons.solution:
for hour in range(6, 19, 4):
    print(f"upload window at {hour}:00")
lessons.hint: The stop has to be past 18 but not past 22, since the range never reaches its stop.

check.expects:
upload window at 6:00
upload window at 10:00
upload window at 14:00
upload window at 18:00

lessons.title: An accumulator that grows every turn
lessons.goal: Add up values across the turns of a loop using a variable created before it.
lessons.theory:
A loop that only prints is worth little. Most loops are there to build up a result: a total, a count, a longest title. The variable that holds that result while the loop runs is called an **accumulator**.

It has one rule and breaking it is the classic beginner bug: the accumulator is created **before** the loop, never inside it. Put `total = 0` inside the block and it is reset to zero on every turn, so at the end it holds only the last value instead of the sum of all of them.

Inside the loop the accumulator is read and written in the same line: `total = total + day * 100`. The right side is worked out first with the old value, and the result is attached back to the same name. The old value has to be on the right of the `=`, or you are not accumulating anything, you are overwriting.
lessons.task: Create `total` with a value of 0 before the loop, and inside the loop add `day * 100` to it, then print the day and the running total on each turn.
lessons.starter:
for day in range(1, 6):
    print(f"day {day}")
lessons.solution:
total = 0
for day in range(1, 6):
    total = total + day * 100
    print(f"day {day} total {total}")
lessons.hint: The line that creates the accumulator is not indented, the line that grows it is.

check.expects:
day 1 total 100
day 2 total 300
day 3 total 600
day 4 total 1000
day 5 total 1500

lessons.title: The same rebinding, written shorter
lessons.goal: Grow, shrink or scale a variable with the short form of assignment instead of repeating its name.
lessons.theory:
In the last mission you wrote `total = total + day * 100`. Read that line again: the name appears twice, once on the right to be read and once on the left to be written. Python has a shorter way to write exactly that, with no second meaning: `total += day * 100`.

`x += 5` **is** `x = x + 5`. `x -= 5` is `x = x - 5`. `x *= 2` is `x = x * 2`. The same holds for `/=`, `//=`, `%=` and `**=`. Nothing new happens: the old value is read, the operation is done, the result is attached back to the same name. It is not a special counter and it does not modify a number in place.

Two things follow from that. The name has to exist already, so the accumulator is still created before the loop with `total = 0`, and `total += 1` on a name that does not exist yet is a `NameError`. And the whole right side is worked out first, so `total *= 2 + 1` multiplies by 3.

You write it the long way once to see the mechanism. After that you write it short, because every codebase you will read uses this form, and a block of `used = used + 30` and `remaining = remaining - 30` is slower to scan than the same block with `+=` and `-=`.
lessons.task: Inside the loop, before the print, add 30 to `used` and take 30 off `remaining`, both in the short form, so every account line shows the running numbers.
lessons.starter:
remaining = 150
used = 0
for account in range(1, 6):
    print(f"account {account}: used {used}, remaining {remaining}")
lessons.solution:
remaining = 150
used = 0
for account in range(1, 6):
    used += 30
    remaining -= 30
    print(f"account {account}: used {used}, remaining {remaining}")
lessons.hint: `used += 30` is the entire line. There is no second `used` on the right of it.

check.expects:
account 1: used 30, remaining 120
account 2: used 60, remaining 90
account 3: used 90, remaining 60
account 4: used 120, remaining 30
account 5: used 150, remaining 0

lessons.title: Counting the ones that match
lessons.goal: Walk a string one character at a time and count only the characters that pass a test.
lessons.theory:
A `for` loop does not need `range`. Give it a string and it walks it one character at a time: `for letter in title:` runs once per character, with `letter` holding a one-character string each turn.

A **counter** is an accumulator that only moves when a condition is true. The shape is always the same: start at zero before the loop, put an `if` inside the loop, and grow the counter inside the `if`. Everything the `if` rejects simply passes through without touching the counter.

Note the two levels of indentation. The `if` is indented because it is inside the loop, and the line that grows the counter is indented again because it is inside the `if`. Get those levels wrong and the counter grows on every character, which is a bug the program will not report.
lessons.task: Count the spaces in the title: create `spaces` set to 0 before the loop, add 1 to it inside the loop when `letter` is a space, and after the loop print the word count, which is the number of spaces plus one.
lessons.hint: A space is a string like any other, written `" "`.

lessons.title: Leaving a loop the moment you have the answer
lessons.goal: Stop a loop early with break instead of running turns you no longer need.
lessons.theory:
`break` ends the loop immediately. The rest of the current turn is skipped, the remaining turns never happen, and the program continues after the loop.

You use it when the loop is a search. Once the thing is found there is nothing left to look for, and every extra turn costs time or quota. A loop written to check seven days of growth does not need day six and seven if the answer appeared on day five.

`break` only leaves the loop it is written in, not the whole program and not the function around it. Do not confuse it with anything that stops the script: after a `break`, the next line outside the loop still runs.
lessons.task: Inside the loop, after the print, add an `if` that checks whether `views` is over 10000: print that the threshold was crossed on that day, then `break` out of the loop.
lessons.starter:
views = 400
for day in range(1, 8):
    views = views * 2
    print(f"day {day}: {views}")
lessons.solution:
views = 400
for day in range(1, 8):
    views = views * 2
    print(f"day {day}: {views}")
    if views > 10000:
        print(f"threshold crossed on day {day}")
        break
lessons.hint: Both the print and the `break` belong inside the `if`, so both are indented under it.

check.expects:
day 1: 800
day 2: 1600
day 3: 3200
day 4: 6400
day 5: 12800
threshold crossed on day 5

lessons.title: Skipping one turn without stopping the loop
lessons.goal: Use continue to abandon the current turn and go straight to the next one.
lessons.theory:
`continue` is the other half of `break`. It abandons the rest of the current turn and jumps back to the top of the loop for the next one. The loop keeps running.

This is how you handle the bad entry in a batch. One account is out of quota, one file is missing, one row is empty: you say so, you `continue`, and the other turns are untouched. Without it you end up wrapping the whole body of the loop in an `if`, pushing everything one level deeper for the sake of one exception.

Anything written after `continue` inside the same turn never runs. That is the point, and it is also the way to lose a line by accident: put `continue` too early and the work below it is silently skipped on every turn.
lessons.task: At the top of the loop add an `if` that catches slot 3: print that slot 3 is out of quota, then `continue` so the ready line is not printed for it.
lessons.starter:
for slot in range(1, 6):
    print(f"slot {slot} ready")
lessons.hint: The `if` goes before the print that already exists, not after it.

check.expects:
slot 1 ready
slot 2 ready
slot 3 is out of quota
slot 4 ready
slot 5 ready

lessons.title: A loop inside a loop
lessons.goal: Nest one loop in another and know how many turns the pair really runs.
lessons.theory:
The block inside a loop is ordinary code, so it can hold another loop. When it does, the inner loop runs **completely** on every single turn of the outer one.

Two accounts with three images each is not five turns, it is six: two turns of the outer loop, three turns of the inner loop inside each. The total is the outer count multiplied by the inner count, and that multiplication is the thing to keep an eye on. Nesting is cheap to write and expensive to run.

The two loops need different names for their variables. If both call it `i`, the inner one overwrites the outer one and the outer turn number is lost. Name them after what they are, `account` and `image`, and the problem cannot happen.
lessons.task: Inside the existing loop, add a second `for` loop over `image` in `range(1, 3)`, and print one line per pair giving the account number and the image number.
lessons.starter:
for account in range(1, 4):
    print(f"account {account}")
lessons.hint: The print moves inside the inner loop, so it is indented twice.

check.expects:
account 1 image 1
account 1 image 2
account 2 image 1
account 2 image 2
account 3 image 1
account 3 image 2

lessons.title: The loop that never ends
lessons.goal: Recognise an accidental infinite loop and cap a loop whose end you do not control.
lessons.theory:
The editor stops your program after 8 seconds and tells you a never-ending loop is the usual cause. It is right almost every time. An **infinite loop** is a `while` whose condition never turns `False`, and there are three ways to write one without noticing:

- you forgot the line that moves the value, so `while pending > 0:` reads the same `pending` forever
- you moved it the wrong way, `pending = pending + 1` under a condition that waits for it to reach zero
- the condition reads a variable that only changes somewhere else, like `while not finished:` with nothing inside ever setting `finished` to `True`

The symptom tells you which. If the same line prints thousands of times, the value is not moving. If nothing prints at all, the loop is spinning without a print inside it. Either way you read the condition, then you hunt for the line that is supposed to make it false.

The third shape is the dangerous one, because the loop is correct and the outside world is not: a render you are waiting for may simply never finish. The cure is a cap. You count the turns and you write the maximum into the condition, so the loop ends by itself even when the thing you are waiting for never arrives.
lessons.task: Add `finished` set to `False` before the loop, and change the condition to `while not finished and attempts < 5` so the loop gives up after 5 attempts, then print how many attempts it took.
lessons.starter:
attempts = 0
while attempts < 3:
    attempts = attempts + 1
    print(f"checking render, attempt {attempts}")
print("stopped")
lessons.solution:
attempts = 0
finished = False
while not finished and attempts < 5:
    attempts = attempts + 1
    print(f"checking render, attempt {attempts}")
print(f"gave up after {attempts} attempts")
lessons.hint: Nothing in the loop sets `finished` to `True`, so the cap is the only thing that ends it. That is deliberate.

check.expects:
checking render, attempt 1
checking render, attempt 2
checking render, attempt 3
checking render, attempt 4
checking render, attempt 5
gave up after 5 attempts

lessons.title: One name, many values
lessons.goal: You can hold a whole set of values under a single name and ask how many there are.
lessons.theory:
So far every name held exactly one value. Real work never looks like that. You do not have one channel, one file or one pending render, you have a set of them, and the set changes size.

A **list** is an ordered collection written between square brackets, values separated by commas:

```python
files = ["a.mp4", "b.mp4", "c.mp4"]
```

The list itself is one value, so it fits in one variable. `print` shows it with the brackets and the quotes still on, because it is showing you the list, not its contents laid out for a human.

The built-in `len()` answers one question: how many items are in there. It works on a list of three strings, on a list of four hundred numbers, on an empty list `[]` where it answers `0`. You will call it constantly, because "how many" is the first thing you ask of any collection.
lessons.task: Below the line that prints the list, print how many channels it holds using `len`.
lessons.starter:
channels = ["Cobly", "Gildo und Weltreisen", "Pluma Waves"]
print(channels)
lessons.solution:
channels = ["Cobly", "Gildo und Weltreisen", "Pluma Waves"]
print(channels)
print(len(channels))
lessons.hint: `len` is a function like `print`, so it takes the list between parentheses and hands back a number.

lessons.title: Reaching one item
lessons.goal: You can pull a single item out of a list by its position, counting from either end.
lessons.theory:
A list is ordered, so every item has a fixed position, and you get one item by writing that position in square brackets after the name.

Positions start at **zero**. In a list of four items the valid positions are 0, 1, 2 and 3. `titles[0]` is the first, `titles[1]` the second. This is not a quirk to memorise and resent, it is the reason the arithmetic in the rest of the language stays clean.

Negative positions count backwards from the end. `titles[-1]` is the last item, `titles[-2]` the one before it. That matters because you very often want the newest record without knowing how many records arrived.

Ask for a position that does not exist and Python raises `IndexError`. That is the same kind of message you met in chapter 0: it tells you the list was shorter than you assumed.
lessons.task: Print the third title using its position, and then print the last title using a negative position.
lessons.starter:
titles = ["Ancient Rome in 10 minutes", "The lost city", "Deep sleep 3 hours", "Why bridges fall"]
print(titles[0])
lessons.solution:
titles = ["Ancient Rome in 10 minutes", "The lost city", "Deep sleep 3 hours", "Why bridges fall"]
print(titles[0])
print(titles[2])
print(titles[-1])
lessons.hint: The third item sits at position 2, because the first one sits at position 0.

check.expects:
Ancient Rome in 10 minutes
Deep sleep 3 hours
Why bridges fall

lessons.title: Taking a piece of a list
lessons.goal: You can cut a range of items out of a list and get a new, smaller list back.
lessons.theory:
One position gives you one item. Two positions separated by a colon give you a **slice**, which is a new list containing a range of items:

```python
queue[1:3]
```

The first number is where the slice starts, the second is where it stops, and the stop is **not included**. `queue[1:3]` gives you positions 1 and 2, two items. That looks unfair the first day and then never bothers you again, because `queue[0:3]` and `queue[3:6]` fit together with no overlap and no gap.

Either side can be left out. `queue[:2]` means from the beginning, `queue[2:]` means to the end, and negative numbers work here too: `queue[-2:]` is the last two items, whatever the length.

A slice always hands back a **new list**. The original is untouched. That is the difference between looking at part of your data and destroying the rest of it.
lessons.task: Print the two middle files with a slice that starts at position 2 and stops at position 4, then print the last two files with a negative slice.
lessons.starter:
queue = ["clip1.mp4", "clip2.mp4", "clip3.mp4", "clip4.mp4", "clip5.mp4"]
print(queue[:2])
lessons.solution:
queue = ["clip1.mp4", "clip2.mp4", "clip3.mp4", "clip4.mp4", "clip5.mp4"]
print(queue[:2])
print(queue[2:4])
print(queue[-2:])
lessons.hint: Leaving the right side of the colon empty means "keep going to the end", so the last two items are a slice that starts at -2.

lessons.title: Growing and shrinking a list
lessons.goal: You can add and delete items in a list that already exists, without rebuilding it.
lessons.theory:
A list is not frozen once you write it. It changes in place, and the name keeps pointing at the same list while the contents move under it. Three methods do almost all of that work:

- `pending.append("publish")` puts one item at the end.
- `pending.remove("upload")` deletes the first item equal to that value, and raises `ValueError` if no item matches.
- `pending.pop(0)` deletes the item at that position **and hands it back**, so you can store it: `job = pending.pop(0)`. Called with nothing, `pop()` takes the last item.

The difference between `remove` and `pop` is what you know. Use `remove` when you know the value and not where it is. Use `pop` when you know the position and want the value.

And note what these return. `append` and `remove` return nothing, they only change the list. Writing `pending = pending.append("x")` throws your whole list away and leaves you with `None`. That is one of the first real bugs you will write in Python.
lessons.task: After the list is printed, take the first job out with `pop` into a variable called `done`, print `done`, then remove the value "upload" and print the list again.
lessons.starter:
pending = ["render", "upload"]
pending.append("publish")
print(pending)
lessons.solution:
pending = ["render", "upload"]
pending.append("publish")
print(pending)
done = pending.pop(0)
print(done)
pending.remove("upload")
print(pending)
lessons.hint: `pop` gives you a value back so it belongs on the right of an `=`, while `remove` is a statement on its own line.

lessons.title: Walking through a list
lessons.goal: You can run the same code once per item in a list without touching positions at all.
lessons.theory:
In chapter 3 you drove a `for` loop with `range`, which handed you numbers. A `for` loop can walk a list directly and hand you the **items**:

```python
for duration in durations:
    print(duration)
```

On each turn, `duration` is one item. No positions, no `len`, nothing to get wrong at the ends. You could write `for i in range(len(durations))` and then index, and beginners often do, but it is more code and it is the version that breaks when the list is empty or when you edit the bounds.

Inside the loop everything from chapter 2 still works. An `if` filters, a counter started at `0` before the loop counts what passes. The counter has to live **outside** the loop, otherwise it is reset on every turn and always ends at 1.
lessons.task: Set a counter named `long_clips` to 0, walk `durations` with a `for` loop, add 1 for every duration greater than 60, and print `f"clips over 60s: {long_clips}"` after the loop.
lessons.starter:
durations = [42, 187, 65, 610, 30]
print(durations)
lessons.hint: The `print` at the end is not indented, because it runs once when the loop is finished, not once per item.

lessons.title: Sorting by something other than the value
lessons.goal: You can sort a list by any property of its items, not just by the items themselves.
lessons.theory:
`sorted(titles)` gives you a **new** list in order, alphabetical for strings and numeric for numbers. The list you passed in is untouched. If you want the list itself reordered, `titles.sort()` does it in place and returns nothing.

Alphabetical is rarely the order you want. `sorted` takes a `key`: something that turns each item into the value that decides its position. Pass `key=len` and the items are ordered by their length, shortest first, while the items you get back are still the original strings.

```python
sorted(titles, key=len)
```

Add `reverse=True` and the same order runs backwards, longest first. Those two arguments cover most ranking you will ever write: sort by the thing you care about, then flip it so the winner is at position 0.
lessons.task: Print `titles` sorted by length shortest first, then print it sorted by length longest first using `reverse=True`.
lessons.starter:
titles = ["Deep sleep", "Why bridges fall down in slow motion", "Rome"]
print(sorted(titles))
lessons.solution:
titles = ["Deep sleep", "Why bridges fall down in slow motion", "Rome"]
print(sorted(titles))
print(sorted(titles, key=len))
print(sorted(titles, key=len, reverse=True))
lessons.hint: `key=len` is written without parentheses after `len`, because you are handing `sorted` the tool itself, not the result of using it.

check.expects:
['Deep sleep', 'Rome', 'Why bridges fall down in slow motion']
['Rome', 'Deep sleep', 'Why bridges fall down in slow motion']
['Why bridges fall down in slow motion', 'Deep sleep', 'Rome']

lessons.title: Values with names on them
lessons.goal: You can store a record whose parts are reached by name instead of by position.
lessons.theory:
A list answers "how many" and "which one". It is a bad answer to "what is the view count of this video", because you would have to remember that views live at position 1.

A **dictionary** stores values under names. It is written with braces, and each entry is a key, a colon and a value:

```python
video = {"title": "Rome in 10 minutes", "views": 18400}
```

You read a value with square brackets and the key: `video["views"]`. Same brackets as a list, but what goes inside is a name, not a position. Order does not matter to you any more, only the spelling of the key.

Assigning to a key that does not exist creates it: `video["status"] = "published"` adds a third entry. Assigning to a key that does exist replaces its value. Reading a key that does not exist raises `KeyError`, which is exactly the message you want when a field you assumed was there never arrived.
lessons.task: Print the value stored under "views", then add a new key "status" with the value "published" and print it.
lessons.starter:
video = {"title": "Rome in 10 minutes", "views": 18400}
print(video["title"])
lessons.solution:
video = {"title": "Rome in 10 minutes", "views": 18400}
print(video["title"])
print(video["views"])
video["status"] = "published"
print(video["status"])
lessons.hint: Creating a key and changing one look identical, you just put the dictionary and the key on the left of the `=`.

lessons.title: Reading a key that may not be there
lessons.goal: You can read a field that might be missing and get a value you choose instead of a crash.
lessons.theory:
The last mission ended on `KeyError`. That is the right answer when a missing key means the data is broken. It is the wrong answer when the key is simply optional: a channel registered this morning has no views yet, and a record exported months ago may not carry every field the newest ones do. The report should not die over that.

`.get` asks for a key without the crash:

```python
video.get("views", 0)
```

If the key is there you get its value, exactly like `video["views"]`. If it is not there you get the second argument, the **default**, and nothing is raised. Called with only the key, `video.get("views")` hands back `None` when the key is missing, which is why you almost always pass a default of your own.

Pick the default that is true for the case. For a number you are about to add up, a missing count really is worth `0`. For a field you are about to print, `"unknown"` says more than an empty line. And absent is not always zero: if you are ranking records, a missing figure should keep that record out of the ranking, not hand it last place with a number it never earned.

There is another way to write this, `if "views" in video:` and then read the key with brackets. That is the right shape when the two cases need two different pieces of code. When all you want is a value with a fallback, `.get` says it on one line and names the key once instead of twice.
lessons.task: Print the views of `video` and then the views of `draft`, both with `.get` and a default of `0`, then add the two together into `total` and print `f"total views: {total}"`.

draft = {"title": "Detras del Enigma teaser"}
print(video["title"])
print(draft["title"])
print(video.get("views", 0))
print(draft.get("views", 0))
total = video.get("views", 0) + draft.get("views", 0)
print(f"total views: {total}")
lessons.hint: `.get` takes two things between the parentheses: the key you are asking for, and the value it should hand back when that key is not there.

lessons.title: Walking through a dictionary
lessons.goal: You can loop over a dictionary and get its keys, its values, or both at once.
lessons.theory:
A dictionary is a collection too, so you can walk it, but there are three things you might want on each turn and three methods that give them:

- `report.keys()` hands you the names.
- `report.values()` hands you the values.
- `report.items()` hands you both, as a pair.

The pair is the useful one, and it is unpacked into two names in the `for` line itself:

```python
for name, count in report.items():
    print(name, count)
```

On each turn `name` is the key and `count` is the value that belongs to it. The two names are yours to choose, the order is not: key first, value second.

That pair has a name. It is a **tuple**: a fixed row of values travelling as one thing, and writing two names on the left of the `in` **unpacks** it into its parts. The shape comes back in the next chapter, where a function hands you two values at once and you catch them the same way.

The order of the turns is the order the keys were inserted. A dictionary is not sorted and it does not pretend to be, so if you want a report in some other order you sort it yourself, the way you did with `sorted`.
lessons.task: Print every key of `report` on its own line with a loop over `report.keys()`, then loop over `report.items()` and print each pair as `f"{name}: {count}"`.

report = {"videos": 12, "renders": 9, "uploads": 7}
print(report["videos"])
lessons.hint: The second loop needs two names before the `in`, because each turn hands you two things.

uploads

lessons.title: A list of records
lessons.goal: You can read a table of records, one dictionary per row, and total a field across all of them.
lessons.theory:
This is the shape almost all real data arrives in: a **list of dictionaries**. One list, one dictionary per record, every dictionary carrying the same keys.

```python
videos = [
    {"title": "Rome in 10 minutes", "views": 18400, "seconds": 612},
    {"title": "Deep sleep 3 hours", "views": 90200, "seconds": 10800},
]
```

Nothing here is new. `len(videos)` is how many records. A `for` loop hands you one dictionary per turn, and inside the loop you read its fields by key. What is new is that the two collections stack: the list gives you the row, the dictionary gives you the column.

When you open a JSON file in chapter 6 this is what you will get back, without changing a line of how you read it. So the habit worth building now is to give the loop variable a singular name, `video` for one item of `videos`, and to pull the fields you need into plain variables on the first lines of the loop. Code that reads `views` beats code that reads `video["views"]` four times.

lessons.title: Ranking records
lessons.goal: You can rank a list of records by one of their fields and report the winner.
lessons.theory:
You have a list of dictionaries and you want them in order by views. `sorted(videos)` will not do it: Python has no idea which field decides. Sorting records directly needs a key function, and functions are the next chapter.

There is a way to rank them today, and it is the one you will keep using even after you learn the other: pull the field you care about into a plain list of numbers, and sort that.

```python
counts = []
for video in videos:
    counts.append(video["views"])
counts.sort(reverse=True)
```

`counts` now holds the view numbers, highest first, so `counts[0]` is the best figure on the channel. To name the video behind it, walk the records once more and print the title of the one whose `views` equals that number. Two small loops, each doing one obvious thing, is better code than one clever loop you cannot read next month.

lessons.title: Giving a block of code a name
lessons.goal: You can define a function with `def` and call it as many times as you need.
lessons.theory:
A **function** is a block of code with a name. You write the block once with `def`, and from then on you run it by writing its name followed by `()`.

The shape never changes:

- `def`, then the name, then `()` and a colon
- the body, indented under it

Defining a function does not run it. Python reads the `def`, remembers the body, and moves on to the next line. The body runs only when you **call** it, by writing `banner()`. Those are two separate moments, and confusing them is the first thing that trips people up: a file full of `def` and no calls prints nothing at all.

Call a function twice and its body runs twice. That is the whole point. The lines exist once in the file and run as often as the work needs them.
lessons.task: Move both `print` lines into a function called `banner`, then call `banner()` twice.

print("=== SIGNAL daily ===")
print("channels: 4")

    print("=== SIGNAL daily ===")
    print("channels: 4")

banner()
banner()
lessons.hint: The two prints go indented under `def banner():`, and the two calls go after the definition, back at the left margin.

lessons.title: Arguments, one function many inputs
lessons.goal: You can pass values into a function so the same code works on different data.
lessons.theory:
A function with a fixed value inside it is worth almost nothing. `report()` below always says the same thing about the same channel. Written that way you would need one function per channel.

Put a name between the parentheses of the `def` line and the function stops being about one channel:

```
def report(name):
    print("checking " + name)
```

`name` is a **parameter**. It is a variable that exists only while the function runs, and it gets its value from the caller. The value you actually pass, `report("Cobly")`, is the **argument**. Same idea seen from the two ends of the call.

A function with a parameter fits inside a loop, and that is where it earns its keep: the loop hands it a different value each turn and the body is written once.

lessons.title: return is not print
lessons.goal: You can tell a function that prints from one that hands a value back, and you can use the value.
lessons.theory:
`print` writes text on the screen. That is all it does. A function whose body only prints gives nothing back to the caller, and in Python nothing has a name: `None`. Store the result of such a call and you store `None`.

`return` is a different animal. It ends the function and hands a value back to whoever called it. That value is real: you can store it, add it, compare it, put it in a list, feed it to another function.

The starting code shows the trap in four words of output. `score_printed` computes 300 and paints it on the screen, but `result` is `None`, because the function returned nothing. The number was shown to you and thrown away in the same instant.

A printing function is a dead end. A returning function is a part you can build with. When in doubt, `return` the value and let the caller decide whether to print it, store it or multiply it by two.
lessons.task: Add a second function `score_returned(views, hours)` with the same body, except that it returns the division instead of printing it. Call it with the same numbers, store the result in `value`, then print `"stored:", value` and `"doubled:", value * 2`.
lessons.starter:

    print(views // hours)

result = score_printed(1200, 4)
print("stored:", result)
lessons.solution:

    print(views // hours)

def score_returned(views, hours):
    return views // hours

result = score_printed(1200, 4)
print("stored:", result)

value = score_returned(1200, 4)
print("stored:", value)
print("doubled:", value * 2)
lessons.hint: Same body, one word different: where the first function says `print(...)`, the second says `return ...`.

lessons.title: Names created inside a function stay inside
lessons.goal: You know why assigning inside a function leaves the outer variable alone, and how to make the value cross.
lessons.theory:
Every call gets its own private set of names. The parameters, and any variable you assign in the body, live there and vanish when the function returns. That private area is the function's **local scope**.

The starting code proves it. There is a `total` outside and a `total` inside. They look identical and they are not the same variable: assigning `total = count` in the body created a brand new local name that happens to be spelled the same way. The outer `total` was never touched, and it still prints `0` after the call.

A function can **read** a name from outside, but the moment it assigns to that name, the name is local. This is not a rule to fight against. It is the thing that stops any function you call from quietly wrecking the rest of the program.

So how does a value get out? The same way it got in, through the door. Arguments go in, `return` comes out, and the caller decides what to do with what comes back.
lessons.task: Change `add_batch` so it takes `current` and `count`, adds them into `total`, prints it and returns it. Then reassign the outer `total` with what the call gives back.
lessons.starter:
total = 0

def add_batch(count):
    total = count
    print("inside:", total)

add_batch(12)
print("outside:", total)
lessons.solution:
total = 0

def add_batch(current, count):
    total = current + count
    print("inside:", total)
    return total

total = add_batch(total, 12)
print("outside:", total)
lessons.hint: The function should take the running total as an argument and hand the new one back, so the call line starts with `total =`.

lessons.title: Default arguments
lessons.goal: You can give a parameter a default value so the caller is allowed to leave it out.
lessons.theory:
Write `=` and a value in the `def` line and the parameter becomes optional:

```
def clip_title(title, limit=30):
```

Now `clip_title("...")` runs with `limit` at 30, and `clip_title("...", 20)` overrides it. Python only reaches for the default when the caller did not supply that argument.

Parameters with defaults must come after the ones without. `def f(a, b=1)` is legal, `def f(a=1, b)` is a syntax error, because Python would have no way to know which value belongs to which name.

A good default is the answer you would give nine times out of ten. It shortens every ordinary call and keeps the odd case possible.
lessons.task: Give `limit` a default of 30. Then print three calls: the existing one with 20, the same title with no limit at all, and the title `"Short one"`.
lessons.solution:
def clip_title(title, limit=30):
    if len(title) > limit:
        return title[:limit] + "..."
    return title

print(clip_title("How the Berlin Wall really fell", 20))
print(clip_title("How the Berlin Wall really fell"))
print(clip_title("Short one"))
lessons.hint: The default lives in the `def` line, written with `=`, and a call that passes only the title will use it.

How the Berlin Wall ...
How the Berlin Wall really fel...
Short one

lessons.title: The default that remembers
lessons.goal: You can spot the empty-list default that keeps its contents between calls, and write the version that does not.
lessons.theory:
A default value is evaluated **once**, when Python reads the `def` line, not again on every call. For a number or a string that makes no difference, because neither can be modified. For a list it changes everything: `pending=[]` builds one list, at definition time, and every call that leaves that argument out is handed the same list, still holding whatever the last call put in it.

The starting code is that bug, complete. Two calls, two different clips, and the second one comes back holding both. Nothing crashed and nothing was reported. The function simply returned data that is wrong, which is the dangerous kind of failure: it gets stored, counted and printed in a report long before anyone notices the number is impossible.

The repair is always the same shape. Default to `None`, which cannot be modified and therefore cannot be shared, and build the real list on the first line of the body:

```
def add(item, items=None):
    if items is None:
        items = []
```

Now a call that omits the argument builds its own empty list, and a caller who does pass a list still gets to use it. Write the guard as `is None` and not as `if not items`: an empty list that the caller passed on purpose is also falsy, and that version would throw it away.
lessons.task: Leave `queue_clip` exactly as it is. Add `queue_clip_safe`, the same function with `pending` defaulting to `None` and rebuilt inside the body, then print its first two calls labelled `"fixed 1:"` and `"fixed 2:"`.
lessons.starter:
def queue_clip(name, pending=[]):
    pending.append(name)
    return pending

print("broken 1:", queue_clip("clip-01"))
print("broken 2:", queue_clip("clip-02"))
lessons.solution:
def queue_clip(name, pending=[]):
    pending.append(name)
    return pending

def queue_clip_safe(name, pending=None):
    if pending is None:
        pending = []
    pending.append(name)
    return pending

print("broken 1:", queue_clip("clip-01"))
print("broken 2:", queue_clip("clip-02"))

print("fixed 1:", queue_clip_safe("clip-01"))
print("fixed 2:", queue_clip_safe("clip-02"))
lessons.hint: The guard is the first line of the body, above the `append`, so a call that supplied no list still has one to append to.

lessons.title: Returning more than one value
lessons.goal: You can return several values at once and unpack them into separate names.
lessons.theory:
A function is not limited to one answer. Put commas in the `return` and Python packs the values together and hands back the pack:

```
return best, worst
```

On the calling side you take it apart with commas on the left of the `=`:

```
top, bottom = extremes(views)
```

That is **unpacking**. The count has to match: two values returned, two names on the left. Three names would raise an error instead of silently guessing.

Use it when one pass over the data naturally produces two facts, like the highest and the lowest of the same list. Splitting that into two functions would walk the list twice for nothing.
lessons.task: Rewrite the function as `extremes(numbers)`: it should also track `worst`, and return `best, worst`. Unpack the call into `top, bottom` and print `"best:", top` then `"worst:", bottom`.
lessons.hint: One `return` with a comma in it, one assignment with a comma on the left, and a second `if` inside the same loop.

lessons.title: A function that changes your data, and one that does not
lessons.goal: You can tell whether a function edits the data you handed it, and write one that leaves it intact.
lessons.theory:
A function has a **side effect** when it changes something outside itself: it prints, it edits a list it was given, it touches a variable the rest of the program depends on. A function without side effects only looks at its arguments and returns a value. Call it a hundred times and nothing else in the program moves.

Both kinds are legitimate. The danger is not knowing which one you just called. Look at the starting code: `drop_first` returns the list you expected, and it also ate the first item of `queue`, the original list. Lists are handed to functions by reference, not copied, so `items.pop(0)` reaches back out and changes the caller's data.

`items[1:]` is the opposite move. A slice builds a **new** list, so the original stays exactly as it was and the function's only effect is the value it returns.

When something is mysteriously empty three steps later, this is usually why. Prefer the version that returns new data, and when you do write a function that modifies its argument, make the name say so.
lessons.task: Add `without_first(items)`, which returns a new list without the first item. Build a fresh list called `second` with the same three clips, pass it in, store the result in `kept`, and print `"returned:", kept` then `"original:", second`.
lessons.starter:
queue = ["clip-01", "clip-02", "clip-03"]

def drop_first(items):
    items.pop(0)
    return items

after = drop_first(queue)
print("returned:", after)
print("original:", queue)
lessons.solution:
queue = ["clip-01", "clip-02", "clip-03"]

def drop_first(items):
    items.pop(0)
    return items

def without_first(items):
    return items[1:]

after = drop_first(queue)
print("returned:", after)
print("original:", queue)

second = ["clip-01", "clip-02", "clip-03"]
kept = without_first(second)
print("returned:", kept)
print("original:", second)
lessons.hint: A slice makes a new list, `pop` reaches into the one you were handed. Compare the last two lines of output.

lessons.title: Docstrings, the explanation Python keeps
lessons.goal: You can write the sentence that explains a function in the place where Python stores it.
lessons.theory:
If the first thing in a function body is a string, Python keeps it as the function's **docstring** and stores it in `__doc__`. It is not a comment. A comment above the `def` is invisible to the running program, while a docstring can be read back, printed, and shown by the editor when you type the function's name.

It is written with triple quotes, on the line straight after the `def`, before any code:

```
def rpm_income(views, rpm):
    """One sentence here."""
    return ...
```

A function without one has `__doc__` set to `None`, which is what the starting code prints on its second line.

Say what the function **returns**, not how it does it. The body already says how, and it will change. What it gives back is the promise the rest of your code depends on.

lessons.title: Handing a function to another function
lessons.goal: You can sort records by any field by writing the key function yourself, and read the same thing written as a lambda.
lessons.theory:
Chapter 4 left this unfinished. You could sort titles by length with `key=len`, but you could not sort a list of dictionaries by views: `sorted` needed something that turns a record into a number, and you had no way to write one. You have `def` now, so you do.

`key` takes a function. `sorted` calls it once per item and orders the items by whatever comes back:

```
def by_views(video):
    return video["views"]

sorted(videos, key=by_views)
```

Look at what is missing there: the parentheses. `key=by_views` hands over the function itself, `key=by_views(video)` would call it on the spot and hand over one number instead. A function is a value like any other, it can be stored in a variable and passed as an argument, and calling it is a separate act you are choosing not to perform.

A one-line function like that is common enough that Python has a short spelling for it. `lambda video: video["views"]` is a function with no name: the parameter before the colon, the value after it, returned without writing `return`. So `key=by_views` and `key=lambda video: video["views"]` sort identically. Use `def` when the function deserves a name, `lambda` for the throwaway one you are only passing in. You will read other people's `lambda` far more often than you write your own.

Then sort the same list again with a `lambda` on the same field, store that in `same`, and print `"same order:", same == ranked`.
lessons.starter:
videos = [
    {"title": "Rome in 10 minutes", "views": 18400},
    {"title": "Deep sleep 3 hours", "views": 90200},
    {"title": "Why bridges fall", "views": 4100},

videos = [
    {"title": "Rome in 10 minutes", "views": 18400},
    {"title": "Deep sleep 3 hours", "views": 90200},
    {"title": "Why bridges fall", "views": 4100},

for video in videos:

A function can call another function. That is how a program stops being one long block and becomes a set of parts: each one does a single job, and a function above them puts the jobs in order.

You already have `watch_ratio`, which turns a video into a number. Add `verdict`, which turns a number into a decision. Then `line` calls both and returns the text. `line` does not compute anything itself, it asks.

The payoff is at the bottom of the file. The loop reads as one plain sentence, `print the line for every video`, and each piece can be checked on its own the day one of them is wrong.

Watch the order of the calls: `line` needs the ratio before it can ask for a verdict, so it stores what `watch_ratio` returned and passes that value on. This is the shape of every program you will write from here.
