lessons.title: Text arrives dirty
lessons.goal: You can clean text that came from outside your program without destroying the original.
lessons.theory:
A string has methods and you call them with a dot. `strip()` removes whitespace from both ends. `lower()` returns the same text in lowercase. `replace(old, new)` swaps every occurrence of one piece of text for another.

None of them change the string you called them on. Python strings are **immutable**: the method builds a new string and hands it back. If you do not store the result, nothing happened. `raw.strip()` on a line by itself is a line that does nothing.

They chain, because each one returns a string and a string has methods: `raw.strip().lower()` cleans the ends first and lowercases what is left.

This stops being cosmetic the moment text comes from outside: a form, a filename, a line someone typed. `"  Cobly "` and `"cobly"` are two different keys in a dict and two different names in a comparison. Cleaning is what makes the comparison work at all.
lessons.task: Build `clean` from `raw` in one chained expression: strip the spaces, then lower the case. Do not touch `raw`.

clean = raw
print(clean)
print(raw)
print(clean == "altos del bosque nocturno")
lessons.solution:

clean = raw.strip().lower()
print(clean)

lessons.title: A path is just text
lessons.goal: You can cut a string on a separator and pull the filename and the extension out of a path.
lessons.theory:
`split(separator)` cuts a string wherever the separator appears and returns the pieces as a **list**. `"a/b/c".split("/")` gives `['a', 'b', 'c']`. The separator itself is thrown away, and the result is a list like any other, so `pieces[-1]` is the last piece and `len(pieces)` counts them.

A path is not a special type. It is text with slashes in it. Cut on `"/"` and the last piece is the filename.

`rsplit(separator, 1)` does the same job from the right and stops after one cut. That is how you take the extension off a name that has more than one dot: `"final.cut.mp4".rsplit(".", 1)` gives `['final.cut', 'mp4']`, so index 1 is the extension. A plain `split(".")` on that name gives you three pieces and no way to know which one matters.
lessons.task: Replace the two fake values: build `pieces` by splitting `path` on `"/"`, and build `extension` from `filename` with `rsplit(".", 1)`.

filename = pieces[-1]
extension = "unknown"
print(pieces)
print(filename)
print(extension)

filename = pieces[-1]
extension = filename.rsplit(".", 1)[1]
print(pieces)
print(filename)
print(extension)
lessons.hint: `rsplit(".", 1)` hands you a list of two pieces, so put `[1]` on the end to take the second one.

lessons.title: Paths are not strings
lessons.goal: You can build a path with the / operator and read its name, stem, suffix and parent without cutting text.
lessons.theory:
A path is text, and treating it as text is how you end up with `output//final.mp4`, or with no separator at all. The standard library has a real type for it. `from pathlib import Path`, then `Path("output/pluma-waves")`, and you have a path object instead of a string.

The join operator is `/`. `base / name` builds a new path with exactly one separator between the two pieces, whether or not `base` already ended in a slash. `"output" + "/" + name` is the habit to drop: there you are the one counting slashes, and the day one side already carries one you get a broken path and no error to tell you.

A path knows its own pieces, so you stop cutting strings to find them:

- `.name` is the last piece, `final-cut.mp4`
- `.stem` is that piece without the extension, `final-cut`
- `.suffix` is the extension with its dot, `.mp4`
- `.parent` is the folder above it, itself a path you can join onto again

They are attributes, not calls: `clip.stem`, never `clip.stem()`. This is the same job you did by hand with `split` and `rsplit` in the previous mission, done by code that already knows the edge cases. And anything that accepts a filename accepts a path, so `open(full)` works exactly as it did with a string.
lessons.task: Inside the loop, build `full` by joining `base` with `name`, then take `stem` and `suffix` from `full` instead of from the raw filename.
lessons.starter:
from pathlib import Path

base = Path("output/pluma-waves")
files = ["final-cut.mp4", "thumb.png", "render.log"]

for name in files:
    full = base
    stem = name
    suffix = name
    print(full, stem, suffix)

print(full.parent)
lessons.solution:
from pathlib import Path

base = Path("output/pluma-waves")
files = ["final-cut.mp4", "thumb.png", "render.log"]

for name in files:
    full = base / name
    stem = full.stem
    suffix = full.suffix
    print(full, stem, suffix)

print(full.parent)
lessons.hint: The join is a slash between the two values, `base / name`, and `stem` and `suffix` are attributes of the path you just built.

lessons.title: Join is split backwards
lessons.goal: You can turn a list of strings into one line, with the separator you choose.
lessons.theory:
`join` is `split` run in reverse. You call it on the **separator**, not on the list: `"/".join(folders)`. That reads inside out the first ten times, until you remember what it is doing, which is placing that separator between every pair of items.

The separator can be anything, including nothing. `"".join(pieces)` glues them with no gap, `", ".join(names)` builds a comma list, `"/".join(folders)` builds a path, `"\n".join(lines)` builds a block of text with one item per line.

Every item must already be a string. `", ".join([1, 2])` raises `TypeError`, it does not quietly convert. Convert first.

This is how you build one line out of many values, and it is shorter and faster than adding strings inside a loop.

lessons.title: A report that lines up
lessons.goal: You can control width, alignment and decimals inside an f-string.
lessons.theory:
An f-string can carry a **format spec** after a colon: `f"{views:>10}"`. Everything after that colon is an instruction about how to print the value, and none of it appears in the output.

Three specs cover most reports:

- `<12` pads with spaces on the right until the field is 12 wide, `>10` pads on the left. Align text left and numbers right.
- `,` groups thousands, so `3821440` prints as `3,821,440`.
- `.2f` prints a float with exactly two decimals, rounding it.

They combine, in that order: `{value:>7.2f}` means right aligned, seven wide, two decimals. A fixed width is the only reason a set of rows reads as a table instead of a pile, and it costs nothing.
lessons.task: Give each field a spec: `name` left aligned in 12, `views` right aligned in 10 with thousands separators, `rpm` right aligned in 7 with two decimals. Drop the spaces between the fields, the widths do that job now.
lessons.hint: Each spec goes after a colon inside the braces, right where the value name ends.

lessons.title: Write a file
lessons.goal: You can open a file for writing, write lines into it and know it closed.
lessons.theory:
`open(path, "w")` opens a file for writing. `"w"` **truncates**: whatever that file held is gone the instant you open it, before you write a single character. `"a"` appends to the end instead.

Use `with`. `with open("queue.txt", "w") as f:` hands you the file as `f` for the length of the indented block and closes it when the block ends, including when something blows up halfway through. Writes sit in a buffer until something flushes them. A short script gets away with forgetting the close, because Python flushes when it tears the file object down, and you will see your lines on disk. The cost shows up elsewhere: a long running worker that opens files in a loop and never closes them runs out of handles, and a process killed outright mid write loses whatever was still in the buffer.

`f.write(text)` writes exactly what you give it and nothing else. It does not add a newline. If you want lines, you write `"\n"` yourself. It returns the number of characters it wrote, which is the cheapest proof you have that the write actually happened.
lessons.task: Open `queue.txt` for writing inside a `with` block, and in the loop store what `f.write(title + "\n")` returns in `written`.
lessons.starter:
titles = ["Deep Sleep 8 Hours", "Rain On A Tent", "Ocean At Night"]

for title in titles:
    written = 0
    print(title, written)
lessons.solution:
titles = ["Deep Sleep 8 Hours", "Rain On A Tent", "Ocean At Night"]

with open("queue.txt", "w") as f:
    for title in titles:
        written = f.write(title + "\n")
        print(title, written)
lessons.hint: The loop has to move inside the `with` block, indented one more level, or the file is already closed when you write.

lessons.title: Read it back line by line
lessons.goal: You can walk a file one line at a time and strip the newline that comes with it.
lessons.theory:
`open(path)` with no mode opens for reading. The file object is **iterable**: `for line in f:` hands you one line per turn and never loads the whole file into memory, which is exactly what you want the day the file is a 200 MB log.

Every line still carries its `\n` at the end. That is why printing a line straight out of a file looks double spaced, and why `line.strip()` shows up in almost every loop that reads a file.

`f.read()` returns the whole file as one string and `f.readlines()` returns a list of lines. Both are fine for a small file and both are the wrong reflex for a big one.

There is no file until something creates it. The program below writes `titles.txt` first and then reads it back, which is also how you test file code anywhere: make the input, do not assume it.

lessons.title: JSON out and back in
lessons.goal: You can save Python data as JSON and load it back as real Python data.
lessons.theory:
JSON is text that looks like a Python list of dicts. It is the format your APIs, your config files and every export you touch already speak, so it is the default way to put data on disk.

`json.dump(data, f)` writes a Python object into an open file. `json.load(f)` reads an open file back into a Python object. The two with an `s` on the end, `json.dumps` and `json.loads`, do the same job with a string instead of a file.

What comes back is real Python, not text: a list of dicts you index with `channel["name"]` and count with `len`. What does not survive the round trip is anything JSON has no word for. Tuples come back as lists, and dict keys come back as strings even if you wrote them as numbers.

    {"name": "Cobly", "subs": 188000},
    {"name": "Pluma Waves", "subs": 37}
]

    json.dump(channels, f)

print("saved")

loaded = []

for channel in loaded:
    print(channel["name"], channel["subs"])

lessons.title: CSV without splitting on commas
lessons.goal: You can write and read a CSV file and get a dict per row instead of counting columns.
lessons.theory:
A CSV is a text file with one record per line and fields separated by commas. Splitting a line on `","` works right up to the first video title that has a comma in it, and then it wrecks that row without an error. Use the `csv` module and let it deal with quoting.

`csv.writer(f).writerows(rows)` writes a list of lists and quotes whatever needs quoting. Pass `newline=""` to `open` when the file is a CSV, otherwise on some systems every row gets a blank line after it.

Reading has two shapes. `csv.reader(f)` gives you a list per row, header line included, and you address fields by position: `row[1]`. `csv.DictReader(f)` reads the first line as the header and gives you a **dict** per row, so you write `row["views"]` and the code survives a new column.

Everything comes back as a string, numbers included. `int(row["views"])` before any arithmetic.

    ["Cobly", "3821440"],
    ["Pluma Waves", "91230"]

    csv.writer(f).writerows(rows)

with open("views.csv", newline="") as f:

    ["Cobly", "3821440"],

lessons.title: Encoding, the day it bites you
lessons.goal: You know why the same text is a different number of bytes and you always name the encoding.
lessons.theory:
A file does not hold text. It holds **bytes**. An encoding is the rule that turns one into the other, and UTF-8 is the one to use.

`title.encode("utf-8")` gives you the `bytes` behind the text. In UTF-8 a plain ASCII character costs one byte and anything else costs two or more, so `len(text)` and `len(text.encode("utf-8"))` stop matching the moment a name carries an umlaut or an accent. `latin-1` spends one byte on that same character. Same text, different size, different bytes on disk. Write it in one encoding, read it in the other, and you get mojibake: `Güldo` arrives as `GÃ¼ldo`.

So pass `encoding="utf-8"` on every `open` you write, for reading and for writing. Without it Python uses whatever the machine's locale says, which is UTF-8 on your Mac and can be something else on a server. That is the day it bites you: the file was never broken, the reader was wrong.
lessons.task: Encode `title` into `utf8` with UTF-8 and into `latin` with latin-1, and pass `encoding="utf-8"` to both `open` calls.

latin = title

with open("title.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write(title)

with open("title.txt") as f:
    print(f.read())
lessons.solution:
title = "Güldo & Weltreisen"
utf8 = title.encode("utf-8")
latin = title.encode("latin-1")
print(len(title), len(utf8), len(latin))

with open("title.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write(title)

with open("title.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read())
lessons.hint: `encode` is a method on the string and it takes the encoding name as its argument.

lessons.title: Read the traceback from the bottom
lessons.goal: Find the error and the exact line that caused it in any traceback, without reading the middle.
lessons.theory:
When Python stops, it prints a **traceback**. It looks like a wall of text and most people
read it top to bottom, which is the wrong direction. The top is the outermost call, usually
something you did not write. The information you need is at the bottom.

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "report.py", line 12, in <module>
    total = add_views(rows)
  File "report.py", line 7, in add_views
    total = total + row["views"]
KeyError: 'views'
```

Read it bottom up. The **last line** is what happened: an error type, a colon, and a message.
`KeyError: 'views'` means something asked a dictionary for a key called `views` that was not there.
The **last `File` line above it** is where it happened: `report.py`, line 7, inside `add_views`.
Everything above that is just the road that led there.

Two lines answer the whole question: what broke, and where. In this traceback they sit at the very
end and three lines from the end, because each frame prints two lines, the `File` line and the code
line under it.

  File "report.py", line 12, in <module>
    total = add_views(rows)
  File "report.py", line 7, in add_views
    total = total + row["views"]
KeyError: 'views'"""

lines = traceback_text.strip().split("\n")

print(lines[0])

  File "report.py", line 12, in <module>
    total = add_views(rows)
  File "report.py", line 7, in add_views
    total = total + row["views"]
KeyError: 'views'"""

lines = traceback_text.strip().split("\n")

lessons.title: Survive one bad value with try and except
lessons.goal: Keep a job running when one item in the batch is unusable.
lessons.theory:
A batch job that dies on item three of two hundred is worse than one that skips item three and
tells you. `try` / `except` is how you choose which one you get.

```python
try:
    number = int(text)
except ValueError:
    print("not a number: " + text)
```

Python runs the body of `try`. If nothing goes wrong, the `except` block never happens. If a
`ValueError` is raised anywhere inside the `try`, Python **abandons the rest of the try block**
immediately and jumps to the `except`. That last part matters: any line after the failing one, inside
the same `try`, does not run. So put the risky line and the lines that depend on it inside together,
and nothing else.

`int("n/a")` raises `ValueError`, which means the type was right, a string, but the value was
unusable. That is the error you catch when you convert text that came from a file, a form or a
scraper.
lessons.task: Inside the loop, replace the `print` with a `try` that adds `int(value)` to `total` and adds 1 to `kept`, and an `except ValueError:` that prints `"skipping " + value`.

kept = 0

for value in numbers:
    print("reading " + value)

print("total " + str(total))
print("kept " + str(kept))

kept = 0

    try:
        total = total + int(value)
        kept = kept + 1
    except ValueError:
        print("skipping " + value)

print("total " + str(total))
print("kept " + str(kept))

lessons.title: The five errors you will meet most
lessons.goal: Name the error from the symptom before reading a single line of the code that raised it.
lessons.theory:
Almost everything that breaks in day to day Python is one of five errors. Learning their names
is not trivia: the name alone tells you which kind of mistake you made, before you open the file.

- **NameError**: you used a name that does not exist. Usually a typo, or a variable defined in
  another branch that never ran.
- **TypeError**: the operation is wrong for that type. `"views: " + 1200` is the classic, text plus
  number.
- **ValueError**: the type is right but the value is impossible. `int("n/a")`.
- **IndexError**: a list position that does not exist. `counts[7]` on a list of three.
- **KeyError**: a dictionary key that does not exist. `row["subs"]` when the row has no subs.

`except Exception as e` catches any of them and puts the error object in `e`. From there,
`type(e).__name__` gives you the name as text, and `str(e)` gives you the message. This is how a
program can report what broke instead of dying.

Five blocks below trigger five errors on purpose and catch them. Every one of them is a mistake you
will make for real.
lessons.task: Add a fifth `try` block that prints `row["subs"]`, a key the dictionary does not have, and catches it the same way as the others, printing `"5 " + type(e).__name__`.

lessons.title: Catch the error you expected, not every error
lessons.goal: Write handlers that separate two known failures instead of hiding all of them behind one message.
lessons.theory:
`except Exception:` catches everything. That sounds safe and it is the most expensive habit in
this chapter. It swallows the typo you made ten minutes ago along with the bad data you were
expecting, and turns both into the same useless line: something went wrong.

A `try` can have several `except` blocks. Python takes the first one whose type matches:

```python
try:
    average = int(row[0]) / int(row[1])
except ValueError:
    print("bad number")
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("no videos yet")
```

Now the two failures have two different messages, and each message points at a different fix. Bad
number means clean the data. No videos yet means the channel is new and the report should say so.

Anything that is not one of those two still crashes, with a traceback you can read. That is on
purpose. A crash you can read is worth more than a silence you cannot.
lessons.task: Replace the single `except Exception:` with two handlers: `except ValueError:` printing `"bad number: " + row[0]`, and `except ZeroDivisionError:` printing `"no videos yet"`.

lessons.title: Guarantee the cleanup with finally
lessons.goal: Make the close happen on the run that dies, not only on the run that works.
lessons.theory:
A `try` has a block most people never write. `except` runs when something broke. **`finally` runs
either way**, whether the body finished, raised, or returned in the middle.

```python
f = open("render.log", "w")
try:
    write_frames(f)
finally:
    f.close()
```

Without it, the close sits on the line after the loop, and a raise inside the loop jumps straight
over it. What is left is a half written `render.log`: two frames out of four, no line saying the run
died, and a file handle still open. A small script gets away with it, because Python flushes what it
buffered when the interpreter shuts down. A worker that keeps running does not: it leaks the handle,
and if that process is killed outright mid render the buffered lines never reach disk at all.
Anything you take, you give back in a `finally`: a file, a lock, a counter you raised before the
work started.

`with open(path) as f:` **is this try / finally, written shorter**. That is what `with` is for. You
used it in chapter 6 to write and read files and nobody told you why it exists: it was never about
being tidy, it was closing the file for you on the line that raised. When an object gives you a
`with`, someone already wrote the `finally`. When it does not, you write it yourself.

Order is fixed: `try`, then the `except` blocks, then `finally` last. `finally` runs after the
matching `except`, and it still runs when no `except` matches and the error is on its way out to
crash the program.
lessons.task: Wrap the loop in a `try`, catch the failure with `except ValueError as e:` printing `"render died: " + str(e)`, and move `f.close()` into a `finally:` block that also prints `"log closed"`.

f = open("render.log", "w")
print("render started")

for frame in frames:
    if frame == "bad":
        raise ValueError("frame render failed: " + frame)
    f.write(frame + "\n")

f.close()
print("log closed")

with open("render.log") as f:
    for line in f:
        print("kept " + line.strip())
lessons.hint: The close is not deleted, it moves: everything that has to happen either way goes under `finally:`, which hangs off the same `try` as the `except`.

lessons.title: Raise your own error instead of returning a lie
lessons.goal: Make a function refuse impossible input rather than hand back a number that means nothing.
lessons.theory:
A function that gets input it cannot work with has two options. It can return something
harmless looking, like 0, or it can stop. Returning 0 is how a wrong number travels: it goes into a
total, into a report, into a decision, and the day you notice it you have no idea where it came from.

`raise` stops it at the source:

```python
if days <= 0:
    raise ValueError("days must be positive, got " + str(days))
```

`raise` ends the function immediately. No `return` runs after it. The error travels up to whoever
called the function, and if nobody catches it, the program stops with a traceback pointing exactly
at this line. Pick the type that describes the problem: `ValueError` for a value that makes no sense,
`TypeError` for the wrong kind of thing.

The caller decides what to do about it. Below, one call is good and one is impossible, and the
impossible one is wrapped in `try` / `except ValueError as e` so the program reports the refusal and
stays alive.
lessons.task: Replace `return 0` with a `raise ValueError` whose message is `"days must be positive, got " + str(days)`.
lessons.hint: The raise goes exactly where the return 0 was, and the message is built with str(days) so the bad value is in it.

lessons.title: Assert the thing your code depends on
lessons.goal: State an assumption in code so it fails at the cause instead of three functions later.
lessons.theory:
`assert` is a sentence about what must be true at that point in your own code:

```python
assert len(numbers) > 0, "average needs at least one number"
```

If the condition is true, nothing happens. If it is false, Python raises `AssertionError` with that
message, right there. The point is **distance**: without the assert, an empty list travels into the
division, and you get `ZeroDivisionError` from a line that is not the problem, or worse, a silent 0
that surfaces in a report next week. With the assert, the program stops at the moment the assumption
broke.

`assert` is for your bugs, not for other people's data. Input from a file, a form or an API is not an
assumption, it is an unknown: check it with `if` and `raise`, as in the last mission. Assertions can
be switched off when Python runs with `-O`, so never put a check you actually need inside one.

`AssertionError` is an error like any other, so it can be caught with `except AssertionError as e`.
lessons.task: Replace the `if len(numbers) == 0: return 0` guard with `assert len(numbers) > 0` and the message `"average needs at least one number"`.

lessons.title: Debug with prints when nothing crashes
lessons.goal: Find which item of a batch corrupts a total, using one print inside the loop.
lessons.theory:
The hard bugs do not raise anything. The program finishes, prints a number, and the number is
wrong. There is no traceback to read because nothing broke: your code did exactly what you wrote.

The cheapest tool is a print inside the loop that shows **the name of the item and the running
value** after each step. Not the item alone, not the total alone. The pair is what turns "the total
is wrong" into "it goes wrong at row two", and that is the whole job. Once you know which item, you
look at that item.

```python
for row in rows:
    total = total + row["views"]
    print("after " + row["title"] + " total is " + str(total))
```

Watch the sequence, not the final number. A total that climbs, then drops, then climbs again is
telling you one row is negative. A total that stops climbing is telling you one row is zero. Delete
these prints when you are done, or they will end up in a log at 3am pretending to be a real message.

lessons.title: Shrink the bug to three lines
lessons.goal: Reproduce a failure outside the program that produced it.
lessons.theory:
A job over four hundred rows dies. You do not debug four hundred rows. You find the one value
that breaks, and you rebuild the failure in three lines that stand alone: the value, the expression
the traceback pointed at, and a print.

That is a **minimal reproducible case**, and it changes the problem completely. You can run it in a
second instead of ten minutes. You can change one thing at a time. You can show it to someone without
sending them your whole repository. And when it stops failing, you know precisely what fixed it,
because there is nothing else left in the file to take the credit.

Shrinking is mechanical: cut the data in half, run again, still fails, cut again. Remove the loop.
Remove the function. Remove every line that is not needed to make the failure appear. The moment
deleting one more line makes the failure disappear, the bug is in that line.

lessons.title: Empty, zero, negative, missing
lessons.goal: Decide what a function does with the four inputs that break every function on real data.
lessons.theory:
Code written against the data you have in front of you works until the day it meets one of four
inputs, and it always meets all four:

- **empty**: a list with no rows, a file with no lines, a string with nothing in it.
- **zero**: a divisor of 0, a channel with 0 videos, a total of 0.
- **negative**: a delta that went down, a count someone stored with a minus sign.
- **missing**: the key is not in the dictionary, the field never arrived.

None of these is exotic. Empty is the first run, before anything has been collected. Zero is a new
channel. Negative is a subtraction of two snapshots taken in the wrong order. Missing is any field
an API decided not to send today. Handle them at the top of the function, one `if` each, and the rest
of the function can then assume the input is sane.

`"views" not in row` asks a dictionary whether a key exists without touching it, which is how you
handle missing before it becomes a `KeyError`.

lessons.title: Code you did not have to write
lessons.goal: You can pull a module out of the standard library and call what is inside it.
lessons.theory:
Python arrives with around two hundred modules already installed. Not packages you download, not something to configure: they ship with the language and they are there the moment Python starts. The word that reaches for one is `import`.

`import statistics` loads the module and gives you a name to reach through. From then on you write `statistics.median(numbers)`. The module name stays in front of the dot on purpose. Six months from now that dot is the difference between reading a program and guessing at it, because it says exactly where `median` came from.

Imports belong at the top of the file, one per line, before any work happens. Importing the same module twice costs nothing: Python loads it once per session and hands you the same object back every time after that.

Inside `statistics` you get `median` (the middle value), `mean` (the average) and `pstdev` (how spread out the numbers are). On a list of view counts with one runaway video in it, the median tells you the truth and the mean does not.
lessons.task: Import the `statistics` module and add one line that prints `median:` followed by `statistics.median(views)`.

views = [1200, 850, 41000, 990, 1100]

print("videos:", len(views))
lessons.solution:
import statistics

views = [1200, 850, 41000, 990, 1100]

print("videos:", len(views))
print("median:", statistics.median(views))
lessons.hint: The import line goes at the very top, above the list.

lessons.title: Taking one tool off the shelf
lessons.goal: You can import a single name out of a module instead of the whole module.
lessons.theory:
`import statistics` puts the whole box on your desk. `from statistics import mean` takes one tool out of the box and puts it on the bench: after that line you call `mean(numbers)` with no dot in front.

Use the second form when you call the same function all over the file and its name is unmistakable on its own. Use the first form when the short name would be ambiguous. Nobody wonders where `mean` came from. Everybody wonders where a bare `get` came from.

There is a third form, `import statistics as st`, which renames the module. It is worth it for long module names you type constantly and worth nothing otherwise.

There is a fourth, `from statistics import *`, which dumps every name in the module into your file. Do not write it. It is the one import that makes a program unreadable, because a reader now has no way to tell which names are yours and which arrived from somewhere else.
lessons.task: Use `from statistics import mean` at the top, then add a line that prints `average:` followed by `mean(durations)`.

durations = [612, 540, 733, 480, 902]

print("longest:", max(durations))
print("shortest:", min(durations))
lessons.solution:

durations = [612, 540, 733, 480, 902]

print("longest:", max(durations))
print("shortest:", min(durations))
print("average:", mean(durations))
lessons.hint: After a `from ... import ...` line the function is called on its own, with no module name and no dot.

lessons.title: The shelf worth knowing
lessons.goal: You know which standard library module to reach for before you start writing one yourself.
lessons.theory:
Most of the code a beginner writes by hand already exists, tested, in the standard library. The skill is not memorising it. The skill is recognising the shape of your problem and knowing which name to look up.

The short list actually worth carrying in your head: `os` and `os.path` for paths and folders, `json` for reading and writing JSON, `csv` for tables, `datetime` for dates, `math` for the arithmetic that is not built in, `statistics` for averages, `random` for picking and shuffling, `re` for patterns inside text, `textwrap` for cutting long strings to a width, `itertools` for combining sequences, and `collections` for containers that are smarter than a plain list.

The one out of `collections` you will use every week is `Counter`, and the line that fetches it is `from collections import Counter`. Hand it a list and it counts every repeated value in one pass: `counts = Counter(niches)` gives you something that behaves like a dictionary of value to count. Then `counts.most_common(1)` returns a list holding the single biggest pair, and `counts.most_common(1)[0]` pulls that pair out of the list.

A pair unpacks into two names at once, the way it did in chapter 4: `top_niche, top_count = counts.most_common(1)[0]`.
lessons.task: Import `Counter` from `collections`, build `counts = Counter(niches)`, unpack `counts.most_common(1)[0]` into `top_niche, top_count`, and print `top:` followed by both.
lessons.starter:
niches = ["history", "sleep", "history", "true crime", "history", "sleep"]

print("uploads:", len(niches))
lessons.solution:
from collections import Counter

niches = ["history", "sleep", "history", "true crime", "history", "sleep"]

counts = Counter(niches)
top_niche, top_count = counts.most_common(1)[0]

print("uploads:", len(niches))
print("top:", top_niche, top_count)
lessons.hint: `most_common(1)` gives you a list of one pair, so index `[0]` to get the pair itself.

lessons.title: A module of your own
lessons.goal: You can move functions into a separate file and import them back.
lessons.theory:
There is nothing special about the modules that ship with Python. Any file ending in `.py` is a module, and its name is the filename without the extension. A file called `channel_tools.py` sitting next to your program is imported as `import channel_tools`, and everything defined inside it is reachable as `channel_tools.something`.

That is how a program stops being one long file. Functions that belong together move into a module, the main program imports them, and each file becomes short enough to read in one sitting.

The Academy runs a single file, so the starting code writes `channel_tools.py` to disk first and only then imports it. That is the one situation where an import is not at the top: the file has to exist before Python can find it. In your own projects the module is already sitting there and the import goes back where it belongs.

Two lines in the starting code exist for the same reason. Python loads a module once per session and remembers it, so `sys.modules.pop("channel_tools", None)` forgets the old copy and `importlib.invalidate_caches()` makes Python look at the disk again. Without them you would edit the module, run, and keep getting yesterday's version.
lessons.task: Below the write, import `channel_tools` and print `per day:` followed by `channel_tools.views_per_day(48000, 12)`.
lessons.starter:
import sys
import importlib

sys.modules.pop("channel_tools", None)

source = """def views_per_day(views, days):
    return round(views / days, 1)
"""

with open("channel_tools.py", "w") as f:
    f.write(source)

importlib.invalidate_caches()

print("channel_tools.py written")
lessons.solution:

import importlib

"""

lessons.title: The line that separates running from importing
lessons.goal: You can write a module that stays silent when imported and still runs on its own.
lessons.theory:
Every module has a variable called `__name__` that Python fills in for you. When you run a file directly, its `__name__` is the string `"__main__"`. When the same file is imported by another program, its `__name__` is the module name, `"daily_report"`.

That single difference is what `if __name__ == "__main__":` uses. Code inside the guard runs only when the file is the one you launched. Code outside it runs every time, including the moment somebody imports the file to borrow one function.

Without the guard, importing a module executes everything at the top level of it: demos print, files get written, a request goes out. You imported one function and the module ran its whole day.

So the shape of a well behaved module is: imports, constants, functions, and at the bottom a guard holding the part that actually does something. Definitions above, action below.
lessons.task: Inside the `source` string, put the `print("DEMO:", summary(2, 9000))` line behind `if __name__ == "__main__":` and indent it, so importing the module no longer prints the demo.

import importlib

sys.modules.pop("daily_report", None)

source = """def summary(videos, views):
    return f"{videos} videos, {views} views"

print("DEMO:", summary(2, 9000))
"""

with open("daily_report.py", "w") as f:
    f.write(source)

importlib.invalidate_caches()
import daily_report

print("report:", daily_report.summary(4, 12000))
lessons.solution:
import sys
import importlib

sys.modules.pop("daily_report", None)

source = """def summary(videos, views):
    return f"{videos} videos, {views} views"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("DEMO:", summary(2, 9000))
"""

lessons.title: Numbers with names
lessons.goal: You can lift the magic numbers out of a program into named constants at the top.
lessons.theory:
A number sitting in the middle of an expression tells the reader nothing. `videos * 0.42` is arithmetic; `videos * COST_PER_VIDEO` is a sentence. The `0.42` is called a magic number, and it is magic in the bad sense: it works and nobody knows why.

The fix is a constant. Assign the value once, near the top of the file, with a name in capitals and underscores: `COST_PER_VIDEO = 0.42`. Python does not stop anyone from changing it later. The capitals are a message to the next reader, and the next reader is you: this is a setting, not a working variable.

The real payoff is the day the price changes. With constants, you edit one line at the top. With magic numbers, you grep for `0.42`, find seven of them, and discover that three were a different `0.42` that meant something else.

Rule of thumb: `0` and `1` can stay where they are. Every other literal that carries meaning gets a name.
lessons.task: Create `COST_PER_VIDEO = 0.42` and `DAILY_BUDGET = 25.0` at the top, use `videos * COST_PER_VIDEO` inside `cost_of`, and add a line printing `left:` followed by `round(DAILY_BUDGET - spent, 2)`.

def cost_of(videos):
    return videos * 0.42

spent = cost_of(30)

print("spent:", round(spent, 2))
lessons.solution:

DAILY_BUDGET = 25.0

def cost_of(videos):
    return videos * COST_PER_VIDEO

spent = cost_of(30)

print("spent:", round(spent, 2))
print("left:", round(DAILY_BUDGET - spent, 2))
lessons.hint: The constants go above the function, so the function can see them when it runs.

lessons.title: Three copies is a function waiting to happen
lessons.goal: You can collapse repeated lines into one function without changing what the program prints.
lessons.theory:
Refactoring means changing the shape of a program without changing what it does. It is not the same as fixing or improving: the output before and the output after are identical, line for line. That is the whole safety net. Run it, keep the output, refactor, run it again, compare. If the output moved, you did not refactor, you broke it.

The most common refactor there is: the same three or four lines appear more than twice with one thing different between them. That difference is the argument, and those lines are a function. Write `def report_line(channel):`, move the body in, call it three times.

The reason to bother is never elegance. It is the fourth copy. With three pasted blocks, adding a channel means pasting a fourth block and hoping you edited every name inside it. With a function and a list, adding a channel means adding a dictionary.

The three existing lines must come out exactly as they do now. That is the proof you refactored instead of rewriting.

lessons.title: Code that hides what it does
lessons.goal: You can rename someone else's variables until the program explains itself, without breaking it.
lessons.theory:
Sooner or later you open a file you did not write, or one you wrote eight months ago, which is the same thing. It runs. It is correct. And it is unreadable, because every name in it is a single letter.

The method is mechanical and it works every time. Read the program bottom up, from what it prints back to where the values came from. Every time you work out what something actually holds, rename it on the spot. `d` is a list of channels, so it is `channels`. `t` accumulates a sum, so it is `total`. The key `"c"` is view counts, so it is `"views"`. You are not improving the code, you are writing down what you just understood so you never have to work it out twice.

Rename in small steps and run after each one. The output must not move. As long as it does not, you can keep going with no risk at all.

The payoff arrives at the end. Once `f(x)` is called `total_of(rows, field)` and the key is called `"views"`, you can see something the letters were hiding: the function is not about views at all, it sums any field you hand it. Bad names do not just slow reading down, they conceal what a program is already capable of.

lessons.title: Comments that earn their place
lessons.goal: You can tell a comment that pays for itself from one that is only noise.
lessons.theory:
A comment that says what the line below it says is worse than no comment. It doubles the reading, and the day somebody changes the code without changing the comment, it starts lying. `# subtract used from the cap` above `left = DAILY_IMAGE_CAP - used` is not documentation. It is a duplicate that will rot.

Good code says what it does by itself, through names. A comment is for what the code cannot say: why. Why 15 and not 20. Why the retry waits before the second attempt and not the first. Why this branch exists at all, when it looks unreachable. That is knowledge from outside the file, and there is nowhere else to put it.

So the test before writing one: could a reader work this out from the code? If yes, delete it and fix the names instead. If no, the comment is the only thing standing between the next reader and a wrong assumption.

The same rule sorts out docstrings from chapter 5. A docstring says what a function is for and what it gives back. A comment says why the code underneath is shaped the way it is.

    left = DAILY_IMAGE_CAP - used
    # if left is negative
    if left < 0:

        left = 0
    # return left
    return left

lessons.title: The Channel File

Every tool you have ever run starts the same way: data arrives on disk, the program picks it up. The final project is one program that grows across seven missions, and this is its first job. It writes `channels.json`, then it reads that same file back and prints what came out.

- `open(DATA_PATH, "r", encoding="utf-8")` to read

lessons.title: What A Channel Is Worth
lessons.goal: Turn one channel record into a video count, a total view count and an average, using a single function.
lessons.theory:
A subscriber count tells you almost nothing. What you actually rank a channel by is what its videos do. Each record carries a `videos` list, and every video in it carries a `views` number, so the numbers you want are already in the file. They just have to be computed.

One function, one channel, three numbers out. `def channel_stats(channel):` walks the video list, accumulates `total_views`, then divides by `len(videos)` to get `average_views` and hands all three back in one `return`.

A function can return several values at once. `return len(videos), total_views, average_views` sends back a tuple, and the caller takes it apart in one line: `count, total, average = channel_stats(channel)`. This is why `return` beats `print`. A printed number is gone; a returned number can be totalled, sorted and ranked later.

`round(total_views / len(videos))` keeps the average a whole number, because a report line with 1010000.0 in it reads like a bug.

lessons.title: The Channel With Nothing In It
lessons.goal: Keep the report standing when a record is missing the fields the report reads.
lessons.theory:
You registered a channel today. It has a name, zero subscribers, no watch hours and no videos, and the export writes it out exactly like that: `{"name": "Detras del Enigma", "subscribers": 0}`. Feed that record to the tool as it stands and `channel["videos"]` raises `KeyError`. The whole report dies over one channel that has not started yet.

`channel.get("videos", [])` asks the same question without the crash: give me the key if it is there, give me this default if it is not. `channel.get("watch_hours", 0)` does the same for the hours. That is the whole fix for the totals, because a missing count really is worth zero when you are adding things up.

The ranking is where it stops being that easy. Absent is not zero. A channel with no videos has no average views, and the moment you let it into `min` it wins worst place with a score it never earned. That is a lie in your own report. So the ranking gets its own list, `ranked`, holding only the channels that actually have videos, and `max` and `min` read from that list instead.

Two consequences of one idea. For a total, a gap is zero. For a ranking, a gap is not eligible.

lessons.title: A File That Lies
lessons.goal: Load the data behind a guard that survives a corrupt file and a file that is not there.
lessons.theory:
The record with missing keys was still valid JSON. The next two failures are not. An export that dies halfway leaves a file full of truncated garbage, and a path you typed wrong leaves no file at all. Both currently take the tool down before it prints a single line.

Move the loading into `load_channels(path)` and wrap it in `try`. `json.load` on garbage raises `json.JSONDecodeError`. `open` on a path that does not exist raises `FileNotFoundError`. One `try` block can carry an `except` for each, and each one prints what went wrong and returns an empty list, so the caller gets a list either way and never gets a traceback.

Returning `[]` instead of crashing is a decision, not a shrug. It says: this source gave me nothing, carry on with nothing. lessons.goal: Collect the report into lines, write it to a file, and put the whole tool behind one entry point.
lessons.theory:
Everything works and nothing is a tool yet. The report only exists while the program is running, and the program is a pile of top level statements that fire the moment anything imports it. Two changes fix both, and neither one invents a new idea.

First, `build_report(channels)` stops printing and starts returning. It builds a list called `lines`, appends every line it used to print, and hands the list back. A list of strings is something you can write, count, test or send. A printed string is only ever a printed string.

Second, `main()` holds the sequence: write the data file, run the self checks, load, build, write. `"\n".join(lines)` glues the report into one block of text and `f.write` puts it in `REPORT_PATH`. Then the tool reads `report.txt` straight back and prints it, which is the only proof that what landed on disk is what you meant.

Last line: `if __name__ == "__main__":` then `main()`. Run this file directly and `__name__` is the string `"__main__"`, so `main()` fires. Import it from somewhere else and `__name__` is the module name, so nothing fires and you get the functions on their own. That is the difference between a script and a tool other code can use.

]

    try:
        with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            return json.load(f)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print(f"missing file {path}")
        return []
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        print(f"not valid JSON {path}")
        return []

def channel_stats(channel):
    videos = channel.get("videos", [])
    if not videos:
        return 0, 0, 0
    total_views = 0
    for video in videos:
        total_views = total_views + video["views"]
    average_views = round(total_views / len(videos))
    return len(videos), total_views, average_views

    total_subs = 0
    total_hours = 0
    total_videos = 0

    for channel in channels:
        stats = channel_stats(channel)
        total_subs = total_subs + channel["subscribers"]
        total_hours = total_hours + channel.get("watch_hours", 0)
        total_videos = total_videos + stats[0]
        total_views = total_views + stats[1]
    return total_subs, total_hours, total_videos, total_views

def average_views(channel):
    return channel_stats(channel)[2]

def build_report(channels):
    lines = []
    for channel in channels:
        count, total, average = channel_stats(channel)
        lines.append(f"{channel['name']:<26} {channel['subscribers']:>7,} subs  {count:>2} videos  {total:>9,} views  {average:>9,} avg")

    subs, hours, videos, views = fleet_totals(channels)
    lines.append(f"fleet {len(channels)} channels  {subs:,} subs  {hours:,} watch hours  {videos} videos  {views:,} views")

    ranked = []
    for channel in channels:
        if channel_stats(channel)[0] > 0:
            ranked.append(channel)

    best = max(ranked, key=average_views)
    worst = min(ranked, key=average_views)
    lines.append(f"best  {best['name']} at {average_views(best):,} average views")
    lines.append(f"worst {worst['name']} at {average_views(worst):,} average views")
    lines.append(f"no videos yet {len(channels) - len(ranked)} of {len(channels)} channels")
    return lines

    print(f"wrote {DATA_PATH}")

        text = f.read()
    print(f"wrote {REPORT_PATH} with {len(text.splitlines())} lines")
    print(text)

    main()
